### testcases/open_posix_testsuite/conformance/interfaces/pthread_rwlock_rdlock/2-3.c  (openposix: conformance/interfaces/pthread_rwlock_rdlock/2-3)
- Category: WRONG  (secondary: WEAK)
- Confidence: high
- Claim under test: a reader with higher SCHED_FIFO priority than the blocked writer acquires the read lock.
- Problem: Same broken set_priority() error check (== -1), so without CAP_SYS_NICE the threads stay SCHED_OTHER and the test still runs. The default glibc rwlock prefers readers and lets a new reader in whenever readers hold the lock, regardless of priority, so the test passes whether or not the priority rule is implemented. It cannot detect a violation of the claimed rule.
- Evidence: 2-3.c:63-73, 153 (default attr), 203-215; man pthread_setschedparam(3) RETURN VALUE.
- Suggested action: fix the error check (return UNTESTED when SCHED_FIFO cannot be set); accept that on glibc this only verifies reader preference, or drop.
- Verification (phase 2, run on real hosts): **CONFIRMED** via RUN,MUTATION. VIRT as uid 65534: Test PASSED (SCHED_FIFO silently not set). VIRT root mutant swapping priorities (blocked writer min+1 > reader min, so POSIX TPS says the reader shall NOT get the lock): still 'Test PASSED' rc=0, reader acquired -> glibc default reader preference passes regardless of priority; the test cannot detect a violation
- Verification (phase 3, glibc vs musl build and libc sources): **CONFIRMED** via MUSL,RUN,MUTATION,SRC. HPE glibc PASS; musl PASS as root and as uid 65534 (no 'Can't set policy' despite EPERM). musl mutant with priorities swapped (blocked writer min+1 > reader min, TPS says reader must block): 'Test PASSED' -> musl, like glibc, admits readers whenever not write-locked (src/thread/pthread_rwlock_tryrdlock.c:8-11)

### testcases/open_posix_testsuite/conformance/interfaces/pthread_rwlock_unlock/3-1.c  (openposix: conformance/interfaces/pthread_rwlock_unlock/3-1)
- Category: WRONG  (secondary: UNDOC)
- Confidence: high
- Claim under test: with SCHED_FIFO waiters, the lock is granted in priority order, writers before readers at equal priority.
- Problem: set_priority() checks `pthread_setschedparam(...) == -1`, which never happens (it returns an error number), so without CAP_SYS_NICE the threads stay SCHED_OTHER. The test then asserts the POSIX TPS ordering, which only applies to SCHED_FIFO/RR/SPORADIC waiters. In addition, glibc's default rwlock is reader-preferring and ignores priorities (sourceware bug 13701, the same non-conformance worked around in rdlock/2-1 with setkind_np), so after the write unlock the reader gets the lock before writer1. Built and run locally as non-root on this system (glibc, Linux 7.2): "Test fail: writer did not get write lock, when test_main release the lock", exit 1, with no "Can't set policy" message.
- Evidence: 3-1.c:63-73 (== -1), 195-196, 299-312; man pthread_setschedparam(3) RETURN VALUE: "on error, they return a nonzero error number"; man pthread_rwlockattr_setkind_np(3): default is PTHREAD_RWLOCK_PREFER_READER_NP.
- Suggested action: fix the error check and return UNTESTED when SCHED_FIFO cannot be set; on glibc either use PTHREAD_RWLOCK_PREFER_WRITER_NONRECURSIVE_NP (as rdlock/2-1 does) or mark it a known glibc non-conformance.
- Verification (phase 2, run on real hosts): **CONFIRMED** via RUN. HPE as root (SCHED_FIFO set OK): rc=1 'reader: acquired read lock / Test fail: writer did not get write lock, when test_main release the lock'; VIRT as uid 65534 (EPERM from setschedparam, no 'Can't set policy' message): same FAIL. Fails on every glibc system because the default rwlock is reader-preferring (bz13701), whatever the priority; the == -1 check additionally hides missing privileges
- Verification (phase 3, glibc vs musl build and libc sources): **CONFIRMED** via MUSL,RUN,REPEAT,SRC. HPE glibc root: FAIL 'writer did not get write lock'. musl root: PASS 1/9, FAIL 8/9 'reader: acquired read lock / Test fail'; musl uid 65534: FAIL, no 'Can't set policy'. musl unlock wakes all waiters (pthread_rwlock_unlock.c:14-15), readers ignore waiting writers (tryrdlock.c:8-11): no Linux libc does TPS rwlock order

### testcases/open_posix_testsuite/conformance/interfaces/pthread_spin_unlock/3-1.c  (openposix: conformance/interfaces/pthread_spin_unlock/3-1)
- Category: WRONG  (secondary: UNDEF)
- Confidence: high
- Claim under test: pthread_spin_unlock() "may fail" with EPERM when the caller does not hold the lock, and the header says the test "will always PASS".
- Problem: Main checks `if (rc != 0) { ...; return PTS_FAIL; }` right after the unlock, so an implementation that does report EPERM fails the test. The later `if (rc == EPERM)` branch is unreachable. On glibc the unlock simply stores 0 and returns 0, so the test PASSes without testing anything. POSIX.1-2024 also made the scenario undefined: "The results are undefined if the lock is not held by the calling thread." EPERM appears only as a RATIONALE recommendation.
- Evidence: pthread_spin_unlock/3-1.c:97-100 vs :112; https://pubs.opengroup.org/onlinepubs/9799919799/functions/pthread_spin_unlock.html DESCRIPTION.
- Suggested action: Drop the test (UB per POSIX.1-2024). At minimum, remove the early `return PTS_FAIL`.
- Verification (phase 2, run on real hosts): **CONFIRMED** via RUN,MUTATION,READ. HPE: PASS as-is (glibc unlock returns 0, 'Did not return EPERM'); VIRT: mutant rc = EPERM (an implementation that reports EPERM) -> 'main: Error at pthread_spin_unlock()' rc=1 FAIL, so the EPERM PASS branch is unreachable; POSIX 2024 DESCRIPTION 'results are undefined if the lock is not held'; Issue 7 removed EPERM
- Verification (phase 3, glibc vs musl build and libc sources): **CONFIRMED** via MUSL,RUN,SRC. HPE glibc and musl: rc=0 'got return code :0 ... Did not return EPERM'. musl src/thread/pthread_spin_unlock.c:5-6 'a_store(s, 0); return 0;', glibc nptl/pthread_spin_unlock.c:29-30 likewise -> no Linux libc reports EPERM; the EPERM PASS branch is unreachable anyway (phase-2 mutant)

### testcases/open_posix_testsuite/conformance/interfaces/raise/1-2.c  (openposix: conformance/interfaces/raise/1-2)
- Category: WRONG
- Confidence: high (phase 1: medium)
- Claim under test: raise() in a forked child delivers the signal to the child, so the child's handler runs and calls exit(0).
- Problem: The parent decides with `if (!WEXITSTATUS(i))` and never checks WIFEXITED. If the child is killed by a signal (for example the raised SIGABRT taking its default action, or a crash), WEXITSTATUS() of a signal-terminated status is 0. That failure is reported as PASS. The header also says the child "returns 1", but the handler calls exit(0).
- Evidence: raise/1-2.c:91.
- Suggested action: Require `WIFEXITED(i) && WEXITSTATUS(i) == 0`.
- Verification (phase 2, run on real hosts): **CONFIRMED** via RUN,MUTATION. HPE: PASS as-is; VIRT: mutant child uses SIG_DFL for SIGABRT so raise() kills the child (core dump, no handler) -> parent prints 'Child exited normally / Test PASSED' rc=0, because WEXITSTATUS() of a signal-terminated status is 0 and WIFEXITED is not checked

### testcases/open_posix_testsuite/conformance/interfaces/sched_getscheduler/7-1.c  (openposix: conformance/interfaces/sched_getscheduler/7-1)
- Category: WRONG
- Confidence: high
- Claim under test: sched_getscheduler(1) fails with EPERM for a non-root caller.
- Problem: Linux performs no permission check in sched_getscheduler, so the call succeeds and returns pid 1's policy. The test treats only `result == 0` (SCHED_OTHER) as "succeeded -> UNTESTED". Any other successful return falls into `if (errno != EPERM) ... return PTS_FAIL`, for example pid 1 running SCHED_BATCH/IDLE/RR in a container, or with SCHED_RESET_ON_FORK or'ed in (kernel line 1011). The test then FAILs a correct kernel with "errno is not EPERM: Success". An LSM denial (EACCES) also FAILs, although POSIX makes the permission conditions implementation-defined.
- Evidence: sched_getscheduler/7-1.c:74-80; /usr/src/linux/kernel/sched/syscalls.c:995-1015 (only an LSM hook, no uid check).
- Suggested action: Treat any `result != -1` as UNTESTED/UNSUPPORTED. Better, drop the test, since Linux never returns EPERM here (sched_getparam/6-1.c is the same idea).
- Verification (phase 2, run on real hosts): **CONFIRMED** via RUN,CONTAINER,READ. HPE/VIRT host (pid 1 SCHED_OTHER): rc=5 UNTESTED 'has successed'. VIRT pid namespace with pid 1 non-OTHER: 'ltprun unshare -pf --mount-proc chrt -b 0 ./7-1' rc=1 FAIL and 'chrt -r 1' -> 'errno is not EPERM: Success' rc=1 FAIL -> a correct kernel fails; Linux never returns EPERM (kernel/sched/syscalls.c: LSM hook only)
- Verification (phase 3, glibc vs musl build and libc sources): **UNCHANGED** via MUSL,BULK,RUN,SRC. HPE glibc: UNTESTED; musl: FAILED 'errno is not EPERM: Function not implemented'. representative rerun of sched_getparam/3-1. musl sched/sched_{get,set}{param,scheduler}.c:7 return ENOSYS by design; musl declares no PS option (sysconf.c:41 =-1, no _POSIX_PRIORITY_SCHEDULING). Test right; no PS gate (suite-wide). Existing WRONG finding not reached.

### testcases/open_posix_testsuite/conformance/interfaces/sched_setparam/2-1.c  (openposix: conformance/interfaces/sched_setparam/2-1)
- Category: WRONG
- Confidence: high (phase 1: medium)
- Claim under test: Higher numeric priority means higher priority under SCHED_FIFO. The father at max priority and a child at min priority each run a counting loop, and the counters are compared.
- Problem: The busy loops `for (i = 0; i < N; i++) count++;` use a plain global `count`. With the suite's `-O2` (open_posix_testsuite/include/mk/config.mk:5), gcc folds each loop into one `addl $N, count`; compiling this file with `gcc -O2 -S` shows `addl $200000000, count(%rip)` and `addl $20000000, count(%rip)`. So no CPU time is ever measured and the ACCEPTABLE_RATIO logic is dead code. On the usual single-CPU (affinity) path, PASS comes only from `child_count == 0`: the child never ran before SIGTERM. If the child does run, it finishes the folded loop at once, falls out of child_process(), prints "This code should not be executed" and exits. The father's `scanf` then hits EOF (returns -1, not 0), and `child_count` is read uninitialized (line 85 declaration, lines 172-185).
- Evidence: sched_setparam/2-1.c:66, :158 (loops), :172 (`while (scanf(...) == 0)`), :185; generated assembly (`gcc -O2 -S` output, lines 490 and 642).
- Suggested action: Make `count` volatile, or replace the counting with a deterministic check. For example, the father spins at max priority on one CPU and the low-priority child writes a shared flag, which must stay unset until the father lowers its priority. Initialize child_count and handle a scanf EOF as UNRESOLVED.
- Verification (phase 2, run on real hosts): **CONFIRMED** via RUN,MUTATION,BUILD. HPE gcc -O2 -S: 'addl $200000000, count(%rip)' / 'addl $20000000, count(%rip)' (loops folded). VIRT debug mutant: child_count=0 every run (child never runs before SIGTERM). Mutant with father demoted to min prio (child preempts it): 'This code should not be executed.', scanf=-1, child_count=1 (uninitialised) -> Test PASSED 3/3
- Verification (phase 3, glibc vs musl build and libc sources): **UNCHANGED** via MUSL,BULK,RUN,SRC. HPE glibc: PASS; musl: UNRESOLVED 'An error occurs when calling sched_setscheduler(): Func'. representative rerun of sched_getparam/3-1. musl sched/sched_{get,set}{param,scheduler}.c:7 return ENOSYS by design; musl declares no PS option (sysconf.c:41 =-1, no _POSIX_PRIORITY_SCHEDULING). Test right; no PS gate (suite-wide). Existing WRONG finding not reached.

### testcases/open_posix_testsuite/conformance/interfaces/sem_close/3-1.c  (openposix: conformance/interfaces/sem_close/3-1)
- Category: WRONG  (secondary: WEAK)
- Confidence: high (phase 1: medium)
- Claim under test: sem_close has no effect on the semaphore's state when sem_unlink has not been called (assertion 3; the header comment wrongly says "if sem_unlink has been unsuccessful").
- Problem: The test calls sem_unlink first and then sem_close. That is the opposite precondition from assertion 3, and the semaphore's state is never examined. It FAILs only when sem_unlink fails, which says nothing about sem_close. Assertion 3 is tested properly by 3-2.c.
- Evidence: testcases/open_posix_testsuite/conformance/interfaces/sem_close/3-1.c:40-50; assertions.xml id=3
- Suggested action: Drop it (3-2.c already covers assertion 3).
- Verification (phase 2, run on real hosts): **CONFIRMED** via RUN,MUTATION,READ. HPE: TEST PASSED as-is; VIRT: mutant with the sem_close() call removed ('if (0)') still TEST PASSED rc=0 -> sem_close is not verified at all; code calls sem_unlink first, the opposite of assertions.xml id=3 ('if sem_unlink has not been called'); 3-2.c covers id 3

### testcases/open_posix_testsuite/conformance/interfaces/sem_init/1-1.c  (openposix: conformance/interfaces/sem_init/1-1)
- Category: WRONG
- Confidence: high
- Claim under test: sem_init(&s, 0, 1) initializes the semaphore to 1.
- Problem: The FAIL branch is `if ((sts == -1) && (val != 1))`. A sem_init that succeeds but sets the wrong value (sts==0, val!=1) PASSes. The test also calls sem_getvalue on the semaphore before checking whether sem_init succeeded. The condition should be `sts == -1 -> UNRESOLVED` followed by `val != 1 -> FAIL`.
- Evidence: testcases/open_posix_testsuite/conformance/interfaces/sem_init/1-1.c:33-47
- Suggested action: Fix the condition: check sts first, then FAIL on val != 1.
- Verification (phase 2, run on real hosts): **CONFIRMED** via RUN,MUTATION. HPE: sem_init_1-1 TEST PASSED as-is; mutant sem_init(&mysemp,0,2) (wrong initial value, sts==0, val==2) still TEST PASSED rc=0 on VIRT -> FAIL branch '(sts == -1) && (val != 1)' cannot catch a wrong value

### testcases/open_posix_testsuite/conformance/interfaces/sem_init/3-1.c  (openposix: conformance/interfaces/sem_init/3-1)
- Category: WRONG
- Confidence: high
- Claim under test: a semaphore initialized with nonzero pshared is shared between processes.
- Problem: Both semaphores are initialized with pshared=0 and are used only by two threads of one process. No process sharing happens, and the counter n is never checked. The test PASSes whenever both pthread_join calls succeed. It then calls pthread_exit() from test_main, so the sem_destroy/return lines never run (the process exits 0 = PASS). The stated purpose is not tested at all. sem_init/3-2.c and 3-3.c are the real pshared tests.
- Evidence: testcases/open_posix_testsuite/conformance/interfaces/sem_init/3-1.c:60-86
- Suggested action: Drop it (3-2/3-3 cover pshared), or rewrite it to use pshared=1 in shared memory across fork.
- Verification (phase 2, run on real hosts): **CONFIRMED** via RUN,MUTATION,READ. HPE: TEST PASS as-is (both sems pshared=0, threads only); mutant with all four sem_wait/sem_post calls in producer/consumer deleted still 'TEST PASS' rc=0 on VIRT -> neither pshared nor semaphore behaviour is checked; pthread_exit() in test_main makes rc 0

### testcases/open_posix_testsuite/conformance/interfaces/sem_init/6-1.c  (openposix: conformance/interfaces/sem_init/6-1)
- Category: WRONG
- Confidence: high
- Claim under test: sem_init fails with EINVAL when value exceeds SEM_VALUE_MAX.
- Problem: On glibc and musl, SEM_VALUE_MAX is 2147483647 == INT_MAX, so `if (SEM_VALUE_MAX >= INT_MAX)` is always true on Linux. The test then prints "Test skipped" and returns PTS_PASS, so it never exercises anything and is still reported as a pass. The non-skipped path also reads errno without checking that sem_init returned -1. sem_init takes an unsigned value, so the check can be made with (unsigned)SEM_VALUE_MAX + 1. glibc's __new_sem_init rejects `value > SEM_VALUE_MAX` with EINVAL.
- Evidence: testcases/open_posix_testsuite/conformance/interfaces/sem_init/6-1.c:28-44; /usr/include/bits/local_lim.h:99 "#define SEM_VALUE_MAX (2147483647)"; POSIX sem_init ERRORS: "[EINVAL] The value argument exceeds {SEM_VALUE_MAX}."
- Suggested action: Use an unsigned value of SEM_VALUE_MAX + 1u, require a -1 return with EINVAL, and return PTS_UNSUPPORTED (not PASS) when the value cannot be represented.
- Verification (phase 2, run on real hosts): **CONFIRMED** via RUN,BUILD. HPE+VIRT: prints 'Test skipped' rc=0 (PTS_PASS) - SEM_VALUE_MAX==INT_MAX==2147483647 on glibc 2.43; small program on VIRT: sem_init(&s,0,(unsigned)SEM_VALUE_MAX+1u) = -1 EINVAL, so the assertion is testable and the test reports PASS without testing it
- Verification (phase 3, glibc vs musl build and libc sources): **CONFIRMED** via MUSL,RUN,SRC. HPE glibc and musl: 'Test skipped' rc=0 (PTS_PASS). musl include/limits.h:69 SEM_VALUE_MAX 0x7fffffff == INT_MAX, as glibc local_lim.h:99. musl sem_init.c:7 compares the unsigned value: musl-clang probe sem_init(&s,0,(unsigned)SEM_VALUE_MAX+1u) = -1 errno=22 -> testable on both, never tested

### testcases/open_posix_testsuite/conformance/interfaces/sem_open/2-2.c  (openposix: conformance/interfaces/sem_open/2-2)
- Category: WRONG
- Confidence: high (phase 1: medium)
- Claim under test: sem_open with O_CREAT|O_EXCL creates a semaphore that does not exist yet.
- Problem: If sem_open fails, the test reports UNRESOLVED, not FAIL. The only FAIL path is `errno == EEXIST` checked after a *successful* sem_open, but errno's value after success is unspecified (and glibc's sem_open makes several internal syscalls). So the claimed behavior can never produce FAIL, and the errno check is meaningless.
- Evidence: testcases/open_posix_testsuite/conformance/interfaces/sem_open/2-2.c:34-49; POSIX errno: "The value of errno should only be examined when it is indicated to be valid by a function's return value."
- Suggested action: FAIL when sem_open returns SEM_FAILED and remove the errno test (or drop it as a duplicate of 1-1).
- Verification (phase 2, run on real hosts): **CONFIRMED** via RUN,MUTATION. HPE: TEST PASSED as-is; VIRT: mutant dropping O_CREAT (sem_open does not create the semaphore) -> 'sem_open: No such file or directory' rc=2 UNRESOLVED, not FAIL; the only FAIL path tests errno after a successful call -> the claimed behaviour can never yield FAIL
- Verification (phase 3, glibc vs musl build and libc sources): **CONFIRMED** via MUSL,RUN,SRC. HPE glibc and musl: 'TEST PASSED' rc=0. musl sem_open changes errno on success paths: src/thread/sem_open.c:79 access() leaves ENOENT, and :118-121 hits EEXIST on a /dev/shm/tmp-<nsec> collision then retries and succeeds -> errno==EEXIST after success is possible, giving a spurious FAIL; check meaningless

### testcases/open_posix_testsuite/conformance/interfaces/sem_open/5-1.c  (openposix: conformance/interfaces/sem_open/5-1)
- Category: WRONG
- Confidence: high
- Claim under test: sem_open fails with EINVAL when value > SEM_VALUE_MAX.
- Problem: `int counter = SEM_VALUE_MAX; if (counter >= INT_MAX) return PTS_PASS;` SEM_VALUE_MAX == INT_MAX on glibc and musl, so the test silently returns PASS without testing anything. sem_open's value argument is unsigned int, and glibc's sem_open rejects `value > SEM_VALUE_MAX` with EINVAL, so the case can be tested.

- Suggested action: Pass (unsigned)SEM_VALUE_MAX + 1 and require EINVAL. Otherwise return PTS_UNSUPPORTED, not PASS.
- Verification (phase 2, run on real hosts): **CONFIRMED** via RUN,BUILD. HPE+VIRT: returns rc=0 (PTS_PASS) with no output at all (counter >= INT_MAX early return); on VIRT sem_open(name,O_CREAT,0600,(unsigned)SEM_VALUE_MAX+1u) = SEM_FAILED errno=EINVAL (glibc 2.43), so the case is testable
- Verification (phase 3, glibc vs musl build and libc sources): **CONFIRMED** via MUSL,RUN,SRC. HPE glibc: rc 0, no output; musl: rc 0, no output (early PASS). musl include/limits.h:69 SEM_VALUE_MAX 0x7fffffff == INT_MAX too; musl src/thread/sem_open.c:109 and glibc sysdeps/pthread/sem_open.c:85 reject value>SEM_VALUE_MAX; probe sem_open(..,(unsigned)SEM_VALUE_MAX+1) = SEM_FAILED/EINVAL under both -> testable, test never tests it

### testcases/open_posix_testsuite/conformance/interfaces/sem_unlink/4-1.c  (openposix: conformance/interfaces/sem_unlink/4-1)
- Category: WRONG
- Confidence: high
- Claim under test: sem_unlink of a nonexistent semaphore fails with ENOENT.
- Problem: `char semname[28];` is never initialized (the sprintf used by the other tests is missing), so sem_unlink() gets indeterminate stack contents, possibly without a NUL terminator. That is undefined behavior. The test also checks errno without checking that sem_unlink returned -1. It passes mainly because glibc maps any invalid name to ENOENT. 4-2.c tests the assertion correctly.
- Evidence: testcases/open_posix_testsuite/conformance/interfaces/sem_unlink/4-1.c:29-38
- Suggested action: Drop it in favor of 4-2.c, or initialize the name and check ret == -1.
- Verification (phase 2, run on real hosts): **CONFIRMED** via RUN,MUTATION,BUILD. HPE: gcc 16 -O2 -Wall: "'semname' may be used uninitialized [-Wmaybe-uninitialized]" at sem_unlink(semname); TEST PASSED as-is; VIRT mutants: semname filled with 28 x 'A' and no NUL (out-of-bounds read) -> TEST PASSED; semname="/a/b/c" (invalid name) -> TEST PASSED: glibc maps any bad name to ENOENT
- Verification (phase 3, glibc vs musl build and libc sources): **CONFIRMED** via MUSL,RUN,SRC. HPE glibc: TEST PASSED rc 0; musl: 'TEST FAILED: semaphore does exist' rc 1. glibc sysdeps/pthread/sem_unlink.c:31-34 maps every bad name to ENOENT; musl src/mman/shm_open.c:13-20 gives EINVAL (embedded '/', empty) or ENAMETOOLONG. Probe: '/a/b/c' glibc ENOENT, musl EINVAL. Uninitialised name passes only by glibc's mapping

### testcases/open_posix_testsuite/conformance/interfaces/sem_unlink/5-1.c  (openposix: conformance/interfaces/sem_unlink/5-1)
- Category: WRONG (phase 1: WEAK)
- Confidence: high
- Claim under test: sem_unlink returns -1/ENAMETOOLONG for names longer than PATH_MAX or with a component longer than NAME_MAX.
- Problem: sem_unlink is called only if sem_open() with the over-long name *succeeds*. glibc's sem_open rejects such names (__shm_get_name -> ENAMETOOLONG), so the test always takes the "Creation of the semaphore failed" path and PASSes without calling sem_unlink. The assertion is never exercised. The NAME_MAX case also builds a component of exactly NAME_MAX characters, which is not "greater than NAME_MAX".
- Evidence: testcases/open_posix_testsuite/conformance/interfaces/sem_unlink/5-1.c:131-155, 177-186
- Suggested action: Call sem_unlink() directly on an over-long name (NAME_MAX+1 component) and require -1/ENAMETOOLONG. Note that POSIX may list ENAMETOOLONG only as a "may fail" error, so ENOENT might also need to be accepted.
- Verification (phase 3, glibc vs musl build and libc sources): **REVISED** via MUSL,RUN,SRC. HPE glibc: 'Test passed' (both sem_open fail ENAMETOOLONG, sem_unlink never called); musl: FAILED 'did not return ENAMETOOLONG' rc 1: '/'+255 chars is a legal name, musl sem_open succeeds, sem_unlink returns 0. glibc rejects only via 'sem.' prefix (posix/shm-directory.c:55-61). glibc sem_unlink(NAME_MAX+1) = ENOENT, musl = ENAMETOOLONG
- Verification conclusion: The phase-1 note about the "exactly NAME_MAX" component is the decisive bug. "/"+255 chars is a legal name. musl creates it, unlinks it successfully, and the test FAILs. glibc passes only because it prepends "sem." (posix/shm-directory.c:55-61, buffer sizeof(SHMDIR)+NAME_MAX), so a 255-character name overflows. On glibc the sem_unlink path is never reached; on musl the test is wrong. - Corrected action: call sem_unlink() directly on a name with a NAME_MAX+1 component, without a prior sem_open. Accept -1 with ENAMETOOLONG or ENOENT: ENAMETOOLONG is "may fail" in POSIX.1-2024, and glibc returns ENOENT (sem_unlink.c:31-34).

### testcases/open_posix_testsuite/conformance/interfaces/sem_unlink/7-1.c  (openposix: conformance/interfaces/sem_unlink/7-1)
- Category: WRONG

HPE: 'Test passed' as-is; VIRT: mutant with the main thread's sem_post() after sem_unlink removed still 'Test passed' rc=0 in 1.0 s (pthread_join returned) -> the thread was never blocked: sem created with value 1 so its sem_wait succeeded immediately; 9-1.c uses value 0

### testcases/open_posix_testsuite/conformance/interfaces/sigaction/12-1.c  (openposix: conformance/interfaces/sigaction/12-1)
- Category: WRONG  (secondary: WEAK)
- Confidence: high
- Claim under test: assertion #12, with SA_ONSTACK and an alternate stack set by sigaltstack(), the SIGABRT handler runs on the alternate stack.
- Problem:  The handler calls sigaltstack(NULL, &ss) and compares only ss_sp/ss_size, which the
  kernel fills from task state (t->sas_ss_sp/sas_ss_size) no matter which stack the handler is running
  on; only ss_flags & SS_ONSTACK depends on the current stack pointer. So the check cannot fail even if
  SA_ONSTACK handling is broken. There is also no check that the handler ran at all: if SIGABRT is not
  caught, the test still prints PASSED (unless the default action kills it).
- Evidence: 12-1.c handler (ss_sp/ss_size compare) and unconditional PASS at end of test_main;
  /usr/src/linux/kernel/signal.c:4464-4468 (do_sigaltstack fills oss->ss_sp/ss_size from task,
  ss_flags = sas_ss_flags(sp)).
- Suggested action: In the handler check (oss.ss_flags & SS_ONSTACK) or that the address of a local lies within [alt_ss.ss_sp, +ss_size); set a flag in the handler and FAIL if it was not called.
- Verification (phase 2, run on real hosts): **CONFIRMED** via RUN,MUTATION. HPE: 'Caught SIGABRT / Test PASSED' as-is; VIRT: mutant with act.sa_flags = 0 (no SA_ONSTACK, handler runs on the normal stack) still 'Caught SIGABRT / Test PASSED' rc=0 -> the ss_sp/ss_size comparison cannot detect a handler that is not on the alternate stack

### testcases/open_posix_testsuite/conformance/interfaces/sigaction/17-1.c  (openposix: conformance/interfaces/sigaction/17-1)
- Category: WRONG  (secondary: FRAGILE)
- Confidence: high
- Claim under test: assertion #17, with SA_RESTART clear, select() interrupted by a caught SIGABRT fails with EINTR.
- Problem: The parent judges the child with `WEXITSTATUS(s) == PTS_PASS` without checking WIFEXITED.
  If the child is terminated by SIGABRT (handler not installed or not caught, or the signal arrives before
  the child's sigaction() because sync is a 1 s select() sleep), the wait status has a zero exit-code
  byte, WEXITSTATUS() is 0 == PTS_PASS and the test reports PASSED. The opposite side of the same race

### testcases/open_posix_testsuite/conformance/interfaces/sigaction/22-1.c  (openposix: conformance/interfaces/sigaction/22-1)
- Category: WRONG  (secondary: -)
- Confidence: high (phase 1: medium)
- Claim under test: with SA_NODEFER, SIGABRT is not blocked while its handler runs, so raising it inside the handler re-enters the handler.
- Problem: The child installs the handler and raises SIGABRT. On success it exit(0)s from the nested handler; otherwise it returns PTS_FAIL. The parent then checks only 'if (!WEXITSTATUS(s))' and never checks WIFEXITED(s). If the child is killed by a signal, the exit-status bits of the wait status are 0, so WEXITSTATUS() is 0 and the test reports PASS. That happens when the handler is not invoked and SIGABRT's default action (terminate/core) kills the child, or when the child crashes. A real kernel bug therefore turns into a false PASS. A child UNRESOLVED (exit 2) is also reported as FAIL.
- Evidence: 22-1.c:88-94 ('if (wait(&s) == -1) ...  if (!WEXITSTATUS(s)) { PASSED }'). POSIX wait(): WEXITSTATUS is meaningful only 'If the value of WIFEXITED(stat_val) is non-zero'.

### testcases/open_posix_testsuite/conformance/interfaces/sigpause/2-1.c  (openposix: conformance/interfaces/sigpause/2-1)
- Category: WRONG  (secondary: OBSOLETE, FRAGILE)
- Confidence: high
- Claim under test: sigpause() restores the original mask (SIGABRT held) before returning, so a later raise(SIGABRT) stays pending.
- Problem: (1) The FAIL outcome is unreachable. The header says "If it is not, set the variable return_value to 1", but the thread only sets return_value = 0 on success. If the mask is not restored, return_value keeps its initial 2 and main returns PTS_UNRESOLVED, so a real conformance failure is never reported as FAIL. (2) If sigpause() does not return -1/EINTR, the thread returns early (line 65) without resetting sem. Main then spins forever in `while (sem == INTHREAD) sleep(1);` and the result is HUNG instead of UNRESOLVED. (3) sleep(1) synchronisation has the same race as 1-1: if the thread has not run sigaction() yet, the process aborts. sem, handler_called and return_value are plain ints shared between threads. sigpause was also removed in POSIX.1-2024.
- Evidence: sigpause/2-1.c:17 (comment) vs 61-79 (no `return_value = 1`), 64-65 (no `sem = INMAIN`), 98-100, 108-113.
- Suggested action: drop with the sigpause group; if kept, set return_value = 1 in an else branch at line 76, set sem = INMAIN on all exits (or pthread_join), and install the handler before creating the thread.
- Verification (phase 2, run on real hosts): **CONFIRMED** via RUN,MUTATION,REPEAT,STRESS,VIRT. HPE as-is PASS; 0 failures in 5 plain + 5 stress runs on HPE and 3 plain + 5 stress runs on VIRT (1 CPU). Mutant 'sigrelse(SIGTOTEST)' after sigpause (mask NOT restored): handler called twice, exit rc 2 UNRESOLVED, never FAIL. Mutant forcing sigpause result to 0: thread returns without sem=INMAIN, main spins until killed (timeout 20 s, rc 137) = HUNG. Both defects confirmed.

### testcases/open_posix_testsuite/conformance/interfaces/sigqueue/7-1.c  (openposix: conformance/interfaces/sigqueue/7-1)
- Category: WRONG
- Confidence: high
- Claim under test: when several RT signals are pending, the lowest-numbered one is delivered first.
- Problem: the handler compares `last_signal >= signo` but never assigns last_signal, so it stays 0. Since signo >= SIGRTMIN > 0, test_failed can never be set and the test always PASSes, whatever the delivery order. The printed order is never checked.
- Evidence: sigqueue/7-1.c:29,36-38 (no `last_signal = signo;`).
- Suggested action: add `last_signal = signo;` in the handler after the comparison, and make last_signal volatile sig_atomic_t.
- Verification (phase 2, run on real hosts): **CONFIRMED** via RUN,MUTATION,GIT. HPE: as-is PASS (34..64). Mutant unblocking with sigrelse() from SIGRTMAX down (delivery order 64,63..34) still rc 0 PASS. Same mutant plus 'last_signal = signo;' -> rc 1 'Test FAILED: A pending signal was delivered...'; fixed test on in-order kernel PASS. last_signal never assigned since 2003 import (c911fa64e3ec).

### testcases/open_posix_testsuite/conformance/interfaces/sigsuspend/1-1.c  (openposix: conformance/interfaces/sigsuspend/1-1)
- Category: WRONG  (secondary: FRAGILE)
- Confidence: high (phase 1: medium)
- Claim under test: sigsuspend() temporarily replaces the mask (SIGUSR2 stays pending while suspended) and suspends until SIGUSR1 arrives.
- Problem: (1) After kill(pid, SIGUSR2) the parent checks `SIGUSR2_called == 1` and FAILs if so. That variable is the parent's own copy, which is never written in the parent, so this check is dead code. (2) The real conformance failure (SIGUSR2 not blocked by the temporary mask, so its handler runs before SIGUSR1) makes the child exit(1), and the parent reports exit status 1 as PTS_UNRESOLVED. A broken mask replacement is never reported as FAIL. (3) Synchronisation is a fixed sleep(3). If the child has not installed its handlers in time, SIGUSR2 kills it and the test reports FAIL ("Did not exit normally").
- Evidence: sigsuspend/1-1.c:44-62 (handler exit codes), 113-122 (dead parent check), 141-145 (exit 1 -> UNRESOLVED).
- Suggested action: drop the dead parent check, map child exit 1 to PTS_FAIL, and synchronise with a pipe (child writes just before sigsuspend; the signals stay pending anyway because the mask already blocks them).
- Verification (phase 2, run on real hosts): **CONFIRMED** via RUN,MUTATION,READ. HPE as-is PASS. Mutation removing SIGUSR2 from the sigsuspend temp mask (the exact conformance bug) -> child exit 1 -> 'Test UNRESOLVED' rc=2, never FAIL. Mutation sleep(4) before child sigaction (slow child) -> 'Test FAILED: Did not exit normally' rc=1. Parent check of SIGUSR2_called reads its own never-written copy (dead).

### testcases/open_posix_testsuite/conformance/interfaces/timer_settime/3-3.c  (runtest: openposix: conformance/interfaces/timer_settime/3-3)
- Category: WRONG
- Confidence: high (phase 1: medium)
- Claim under test: setting it_value = 0 disarms "a currently armed and blocked timer".
- Problem: The timer is a one-shot 10ms timer (it_interval 0) and the test sleeps 1s before disarming, so the timer has already expired and is no longer armed; only its signal is pending. The handler is installed and the pending signal is (or is not) delivered during sigprocmask(SIG_UNBLOCK) before the final nanosleep starts, so nanosleep is never interrupted either way. The test passes whether or not timer_settime() with zero it_value disarms anything.
- Evidence: 3-3.c:67-79 (10ms one-shot, sleep 1s), 98-107 (disarm), 110-126 (unblock then nanosleep).
- Suggested action: use a periodic timer (e.g. it_value 10ms, it_interval 100ms) so it is still armed when disarmed, then verify no further signal arrives after the pending one is consumed (sigtimedwait), or drop as covered by 3-2.
- Verification (phase 2, run on real hosts): **CONFIRMED** via RUN,MUTATION,READ. HPE as-is PASS. Mutation deleting the disarming timer_settime(it_value=0) call still PASS ('OK to be in once' printed at unblock, then nanosleep not interrupted). The 10 ms one-shot timer has expired before the disarm; kernel timer_settime only bumps it_signal_seq so the stale signal is dropped. The check is vacuous.

### testcases/open_posix_testsuite/functional/mqueues/send_rev_1.c  (openposix: functional/mqueues/send_rev_1)
- Category: WRONG  (secondary: WEAK)
- Confidence: high
- Claim under test: two processes can read/write the same message queue at the same time.
- Problem: The child sets ret_code=PTS_UNRESOLVED on mq_receive failure and exit()s with it,
  but the parent does `(void)wait(NULL)` and returns its own ret_code, so a receive failure in
  the child is never reported. The received payloads are only printed, never compared with what
  was sent.
- Evidence: send_rev_1.c child branch `exit(ret_code)`; parent `(void)wait(NULL); ... return ret_code;`
- Suggested action: wait(&status) and fold the child status in; strcmp received vs sent messages.
- Verification (phase 2, run on real hosts): **CONFIRMED** via RUN,MUTATION. HPE as-is PASS. Mutant with child mq_receive buffer size 1 (EMSGSIZE): child prints 'mq_receive doesn't return success' and exits PTS_UNRESOLVED, parent still rc=0 PASS (wait(NULL) discards the status). Received payloads are only printed, never compared with what was sent.

### testcases/open_posix_testsuite/functional/semaphores/sem_lock.c  (openposix: functional/semaphores/sem_lock)
- Category: WRONG  (secondary: FRAGILE)
- Confidence: high
- Claim under test: a semaphore protects a critical section between several processes.
- Problem: The sem_t is allocated with malloc() and sem_init(..., pshared=1, 1); after fork()
  every process has its own private copy of the semaphore, so there is no cross-process
  exclusion at all. POSIX: a pshared semaphore is usable by any process "that can access the
  semaphore", which requires it to live in shared memory. Nothing is verified (output is only
  printed), so the test always passes. The fork loop lets children continue the loop, creating
  2^(num-1) processes (16 by default), each parent sleeping 2 s per fork; children are never
  reaped and their status is ignored. SEM_NAME is unused.
- Evidence: sem_lock.c: `sem_lock = malloc(sizeof(sem_t)); sem_init(sem_lock, shared, value)`;
  `for (i = 1; i < num; i++) switch (fork()) { case 0: break; default: sleep(2); }`;
  sem_init(3): "If pshared is nonzero, then the semaphore is shared between processes, and
  should be located in a region of shared memory".
- Suggested action: allocate the semaphore with mmap(MAP_SHARED|MAP_ANONYMOUS), have children
  increment a shared counter non-atomically inside the critical section and check the total,
  fork in a flat loop and wait for every child; or drop.
- Verification (phase 2, run on real hosts): **CONFIRMED** via RUN,MUTATION. HPE as-is PASS, 160 lines from 16 distinct pids (2^(5-1) processes). Mutation deleting sem_post() still PASS with all 16 processes entering the 'critical section' (160 lines): each has a private copy-on-write malloc'd sem_t, so there is no cross-process exclusion and nothing is checked.

### testcases/open_posix_testsuite/functional/timers/clocks/twopsetclock.c  (openposix: functional/timers/clocks/twopsetclock)
- Category: WRONG  (secondary: FRAGILE)
- Confidence: high
- Claim under test: two processes setting CLOCK_REALTIME concurrently both succeed and the later
  setting takes effect (clock ends near TESTTIME +/- DELTA).
- Problem: The pass condition is `(delta <= ACCEPTABLEDELTA - DELTA) || (delta <= ACCEPTABLEDELTA
  + DELTA)`, i.e. just `delta <= 6`: there is no lower bound, so any clock value before
  TESTTIME+9s passes, and the "later one wins" claim is not tested. clock_settime() failures
  (EPERM without CAP_SYS_TIME) are only printed as "Note", after which the clock is far past
  TESTTIME and the test reports FAIL instead of UNRESOLVED. The child returns PTS_UNRESOLVED
  from test_main and is never waited for. The final reset uses the time captured before the
  3 s sleep, setting the system clock back ~3 s.
- Evidence: twopsetclock.c pass condition; `if (clock_settime(...) != 0) printf("Note: ...")`;
  clock_settime(2): EPERM "does not have permission to set the clock indicated".
- Suggested action: return UNRESOLVED when clock_settime fails, check
  `abs(delta - DELTA) <= 1 || abs(delta + DELTA) <= 1`, wait for the child, restore
  saved time + elapsed (CLOCK_MONOTONIC).
- Verification (phase 2, run on real hosts): **CONFIRMED** via RUN,MUTATION. Not run as root (it steps the shared hosts' clock to 2002). Mutation with clock_settime no-op'd and tpget forced 1000 s before both settings -> 'Test PASSED' (no lower bound). Unmodified binary as nobody (setpriv, no CAP_SYS_TIME): 'Note: clock_settime() failed' x2, 'Need to manually reset time', 'Test FAILED' rc=1 instead of UNRESOLVED.

### testcases/open_posix_testsuite/functional/timers/timers/twoptimers.c  (openposix: functional/timers/timers/twoptimers)
- Category: WRONG
- Confidence: high
- Claim under test: timers in two processes set to the same absolute time both expire.
- Problem: The child returns CHILDPASS (1) on success, PTS_FAIL (1) on wrong signal and
  PTS_UNRESOLVED (2) on setup errors; the parent passes on `WEXITSTATUS(i) != 0`. So every
  child outcome except exit(0) is a PASS, and the child's FAIL is indistinguishable from
  success. The claim "expire at the same time" is not measured.
- Evidence: twoptimers.c `#define CHILDPASS 1`; child `return PTS_FAIL;` / `return
  PTS_UNRESOLVED;`; parent `if (WEXITSTATUS(i)) { printf("Test PASSED\n"); ...`.
- Suggested action: child exits PTS_PASS (0) on success; parent requires
  WIFEXITED && WEXITSTATUS == PTS_PASS.
- Verification (phase 2, run on real hosts): **CONFIRMED** via RUN,MUTATION. HPE as-is PASS. Mutation making the child's timer_create fail (invalid clock): child prints 'timer_create() did not return success: Invalid argument' and returns PTS_UNRESOLVED, parent prints 'Test PASSED' rc=0, because any non-zero child status is treated as pass (CHILDPASS==PTS_FAIL==1).

### testcases/open_posix_testsuite/stress/threads/sem_init/s-c1.c  (openposix: stress/threads/sem_init/s-c1)
- Category: WRONG  (secondary: OBSOLETE, FRAGILE)
- Confidence: high
- Claim under test: sem_init duration does not grow with the number of semaphores; the test
  fails if the latency trend is non-constant or the final failure is unexpected.
- Problem: The block-filling loop is mis-bracketed (s-c1.c:178-262). The "link block into list +
  append measure" code sits inside `for (i...)`, so after every successful sem_init the same
  block is relinked. From i=1 on, `sems_tmp->prev = sems_cur` makes the block point to itself.
  `nsem++` sits inside the `if (ret != 0)` error branch, so it never increments on success.
  Cleanup then loops `while (sems_cur != &sems)` on the self-linked block, re-destroying it.
  Meanwhile `m_cur = m_cur->prev` runs past the sentinel, and the write through a NULL m_cur
  crashes. Built by hand with gcc and run, it dies with SIGSEGV within
  seconds. PASSED is also inside `while (1)`. The scalability verdict uses
  r1 > 1.1*r2 (constant vs. least-squares linear fit). The linear fit never has a larger
  residual than the constant model, so ordinary timing noise or trend can trigger FAILED.
  Not built in LTP anyway (no stress/threads/Makefile).
- Evidence: s-c1.c:155 `while (1)`, :178-262 (for-loop body), :280-320 (cleanup),
  :360 status check, :730-732 (thresholds); local run:
  "Segmentation fault ... exit=139".
- Suggested action: Drop (the broken code has never run in LTP). A rewrite would need
  correct bracing and a non-statistical pass criterion.
- Verification (phase 2, run on real hosts): **CONFIRMED** via RUN,BUILD. Never built: stress/threads has no Makefile so stress/Makefile's */Makefile loop skips it; HPE logfile.stress-all has 0 stress/threads entries, no binary in /opt/ltp. Built manually on HPE (gcc ... -lcommon -lrt -pthread -lm) and run: 'timeout: the monitored command dumped core', rc=139 (SIGSEGV) within seconds.

### testcases/open_posix_testsuite/stress/threads/sem_open/s-c1.c  (openposix: stress/threads/sem_open/s-c1)
- Category: WRONG  (secondary: OBSOLETE, FRAGILE)

  `if (status) UNRESOLVED`, :728-730 (thresholds).

Built manually and run in a private mount ns with a 1 MB tmpfs on /dev/shm (to cap the unbounded sem_open loop safely): ended with 'FAILED: The function is not scalable' after hitting ENOSPC. ### testcases/realtime/func/async_handler/async_handler_jk.c  (realtime profile: func/async_handler async_handler_jk -c 100)
- Category: WRONG  (secondary: FRAGILE, WEAK)
- Confidence: high
- Claim under test: An async event server thread (FIFO 83) woken by a user thread (FIFO 43) runs its
  handler within 100us.
- Problem: (1) main() computes `delta = end - start` right after join_thread(user_id). Nothing waits
  for the server to have run handler1(): the server is pthread_detach()ed and join_threads() cannot
  join it. On SMP the server wakes on another CPU and `end` may still be 0, giving a negative delta and
  "Result: PASS". (2) user_thread clears THREAD_FLAG_SUSPENDED and broadcasts without holding
  server->mutex. The server tests the flag under the mutex and then calls pthread_cond_wait, so the
  wakeup can be lost. The flag can also be cleared before the server's own
  `thread->flags |= THREAD_FLAG_SUSPENDED` runs: the usleep(1000) in main runs after both threads are
  created and orders nothing. Either way the handler never runs, end stays 0, and the result is "PASS".
  (3) Only one sample is taken, and main returns 0 even when it prints FAIL.
  (4) join_threads() calls pthread_join on a detached thread, which POSIX makes undefined.
- Evidence: async_handler_jk.c:86-104 (server), :107-123 (user, no mutex), :139-160 (no wait for
  handler, delta printed); lib/librttest.c:395-405 (join_threads joins every listed thread).
- Suggested action: Clear the flag and broadcast under server->mutex. Have main wait for an "handled"
  flag or condition (with timeout -> FAIL) before reading `end`. Take many samples. Or drop the test:
  async_handler.c already covers cond-signal wakeup latency.
- Verification (phase 2, run on real hosts): **CONFIRMED** via RUN,MUTATION. HPE as-is 3/3 'delta = 29..48 us Result: PASS'. Mutation removing the pthread_cond_broadcast (server never woken, handler1 never runs): 3/3 'delta = -3874644071 us', 'Result: PASS', exit 0. main never waits for the handler; end==0 gives a negative delta that passes.

### testcases/realtime/func/pi-tests/testpi-5.c  (runtest: realtime profiles/default func/pi-tests testpi-5)
- Category: WRONG  (secondary: UNDEF, WEAK)
- Confidence: high (phase 1: medium)
- Claim under test: "verifies if a thread can lock the priority inheritance mutex multiple times".
- Problem: The child locks a default-type PI mutex twice; PASS is printed only when the 20s alarm in test-skeleton.c kills the hung child. Relocking a PTHREAD_MUTEX_DEFAULT mutex is undefined per POSIX; the kernel returns -EDEADLK for FUTEX_LOCK_PI by the owner and glibc chooses to block forever. If the implementation instead returned an error, the second lock "fails" and the child exits: no Result line and exit 0, i.e. no FAIL is ever reported. The description says the opposite of what is checked (it expects a deadlock, not multiple locking).
- Evidence: testpi-5.c:46-63 (double lock), :94 (#include "test-skeleton.c"); test-skeleton.c:72-122; kernel/futex/pi.c:606-609 (return -EDEADLK); POSIX pthread_mutex_lock: "If the mutex type is PTHREAD_MUTEX_DEFAULT, attempting to recursively lock the mutex results in undefined behavior."
- Suggested action: Use PTHREAD_MUTEX_ERRORCHECK and expect EDEADLK (or RECURSIVE and expect success), or drop.
- Verification (phase 2, run on real hosts): **CONFIRMED** via RUN,MUTATION,READ. VIRT as-is: child hangs on 2nd lock, after 20s 'Result:PASS', rc=1. HPE work copy with PTHREAD_MUTEX_ERRORCHECK: 2nd lock returns 35 (EDEADLK, kernel futex_lock_pi owner check), child exits, no Result line, rc=0 -> PASS means 'glibc deadlocks on UB relock', any other behavior yields no FAIL; description says the opposite
- Verification (phase 3, glibc vs musl build and libc sources): **CONFIRMED** via RUN,MUSL,SRC. HPE glibc: child hangs, 20s alarm, 'Result:PASS' rc=1; musl: same 'Result:PASS' rc=1. Both libcs block forever on owner relock of a NORMAL PI mutex: glibc nptl/pthread_mutex_lock.c:419-431 ('Delay the thread indefinitely'), musl src/thread/pthread_mutex_timedlock.c:48-52 (EDEADLK returned only for ERRORCHECK, else wait forever). PASS = 'libc deadlocks on UB'

### testcases/realtime/func/sched_football/sched_football.c  (runtest: sched/sched_football)
- Category: WRONG  (secondary: FRAGILE)
- Confidence: high (phase 1: medium)
- Claim under test: lower-priority FIFO "offense" threads never run while higher-priority "defense" threads are runnable (strict RT priority on SMP).
- Problem: game_over is set to 1 at the end of referee() and never reset. With -i N (or any second iteration), the new defense/offense/fan threads see game_over==1 right after kickoff and exit; the_ball stays 0 and TST_EXP_EXPR(final_ball == 0) passes without anything having been tested. The earlier threads are also never joined. Secondary: "offense never increments the ball" is stronger than what the kernel guarantees: with RT_PUSH_IPI (default on PREEMPT_RT) pull_rt_task() only IPIs the overloaded CPU and returns, so a CPU whose fan just slept can briefly pick a local offense thread before the preempted defense thread is pushed to it.
- Evidence: sched_football.c:48,147 (game_over set, never cleared), :153-200 (do_test resets only kickoff_flag), :88-104 (loops exit on game_over), :150; kernel/sched/features.h:104-123 (RT_PUSH_IPI default true only for PREEMPT_RT), kernel/sched/rt.c pull_rt_task() "tell_cpu_to_push(this_rq); return;".
- Suggested action: Reset game_over (and the_ball) at the start of do_test and join the threads at the end; document/tolerate the RT_PUSH_IPI window or TCONF on it.
- Verification (phase 2, run on real hosts): **CONFIRMED** via RUN,MUTATION,VIRT,GIT. VIRT work copy with offense prio 60 (above fans): -i 2 -> iter1 'Final ball position: 390027758' TFAIL, iter2 'Final ball position: 0' TPASS (game_over never reset, since e523ba88dd9b). Extra: offense at 45 (above defense, below fans) still ball 0 on HPE and VIRT: 2N fans at prio 50 saturate all CPUs, so defense never matters

### testcases/realtime/func/thread_clock/tc-2.c  (runtest: realtime profiles/default func/thread_clock "tc-2 -c 0.5")
- Category: WRONG
- Confidence: high
- Claim under test: per-thread CPU clocks (CLOCK_THREAD_CPUTIME_ID) of 2 busy and 5 sleeping threads sum to the process CPU clock (CLOCK_PROCESS_CPUTIME_ID) within 0.5s.
- Problem: work() is `for (unsigned i = 0; i < 2147483600; i++) if (i == i + 1 || i == i - 1) printf(...)`; the condition is always false for unsigned and the loop has no side effects, so GCC at LTP's default -O2 compiles work() to a bare `ret` (verified: gcc -O2 -fno-strict-aliasing output is just `ret`). Worker threads therefore accumulate ~0 CPU time, all clocks are ~0, and |process - sum(threads)| < 0.5s holds trivially. The test cannot detect broken thread/process CPU-time accounting.
- Evidence: tc-2.c:80-87 (work()), :155-171 (comparison); include/mk/config.mk OPT_CFLAGS ?= -O2.
- Suggested action: Make the loop observable (volatile counter or busy-loop until CLOCK_THREAD_CPUTIME_ID reaches e.g. 1s) and also assert each worker's clock is close to the expected busy time.
- Verification (phase 2, run on real hosts): **CONFIRMED** via RUN,MUTATION,BUILD,VIRT. objdump of built tc-2: work() = bare 'ret'. As-is HPE: Process 0.0032 s, Threads 0.0006 s, PASS; VIRT: Process 0.0020 s, PASS. Work copy summing worker clocks as 0*(...) (i.e. thread accounting ignored): VIRT Process 0.0018 Threads 0.0001 Delta 0.0017 -> Result: PASS (also PASS on HPE) -> comparison cannot detect broken accounting


#### Grouped entries (WRONG)

### testcases/open_posix_testsuite/functional/mqueues/send_rev_2.c, stress/mqueues/multi_send_rev_1.c, stress/mqueues/multi_send_rev_2.c  (openposix: functional/mqueues/send_rev_2, stress/mqueues/multi_send_rev_1, multi_send_rev_2)
- Category: WRONG  (secondary: FRAGILE / UNDEF)
- Confidence: high
- Claim under test: threads send/receive on message queues concurrently; "set different
  priority to the messages ... to see whether the highest priority is received first".
- Problem: (1) All threads report failure via pthread_exit((void *)1) but main joins with
  pthread_join(t, NULL) and unconditionally returns PTS_PASS, so the tests cannot fail.
  (2) The priority-ordering claim is never checked (received messages are only printed).
  (3) Queues are opened O_NONBLOCK and receivers start concurrently with senders, so
  mq_receive can legitimately return EAGAIN on an empty queue; if failures were propagated this
  would be a false FAIL. (4) multi_send_rev_1/2 call mq_send(q, s_msg_ptr[i], MSG_SIZE /*128*/,
  ...) with 9-11 byte string literals, reading past the end of the literal (C UB).
- Evidence: send_rev_2.c test_main `pthread_join(send1, NULL) ... return PTS_PASS;`;
  multi_send_rev_1.c msend(): `mq_send(send_info.mqID, s_msg_ptr[i], MSG_SIZE, i)`; mreceive()
  even calls pthread_exit(NULL) on error. Stress variants are run with arg "1" (*.args).
- Suggested action: open without O_NONBLOCK (or send before starting receivers), collect thread
  return values, verify that messages come out in priority order, send strlen()+1 bytes.
  Otherwise drop as duplicates of conformance/interfaces/mq_send|mq_receive.


## UNDOC: Relies on undocumented or implementation-specific behavior

The test demands behavior that no man page, kernel document or standard promises: errno precedence when several error conditions apply, internal limits, ordering, exact strings. The kernel could change legitimately and the test would fail without any kernel bug. Action: relax the check to the documented contract, or document the dependency with a kernel reference, or drop the subcase.

24 testcases. Sorted by path; confidence shown in each entry.

### testcases/kernel/mem/tunable/max_map_count.c  (runtest: mm/max_map_count)
- Category: UNDOC
- Confidence: high
- Claim under test: a process can have at most /proc/sys/vm/max_map_count memory map areas.
- Problem: the test TPASSes only if the number of lines in /proc/pid/maps is exactly
  max_maps + 1 and TFAILs on max_maps. That depends on the kernel's off-by-one check
  `mm->map_count > sysctl_max_map_count` (it should be `>=`). The test's own comment
  (l.173-177) says this is "the mm failure point at the time of writing this COMMENT!".
  The documented limit is "the maximum number of memory map areas a process may have". If the kernel
  changed the check to `>=`, which matches the docs (nommu.c and split paths in vma.c:640
  already use `>=`), the test would FAIL. It also depends on every
  /proc/pid/maps line matching one counted VMA, apart from a hand-kept per-arch filter
  for vsyscall/vdso.
- Evidence: max_map_count.c:178; /usr/src/linux/mm/mmap.c:381 and mm/vma.c:3031
  (`if (mm->map_count > get_sysctl_max_map_count()) return -ENOMEM;`), compare mm/vma.c:640 and
  mm/nommu.c:1039 (`>=`); Documentation/admin-guide/sysctl/vm.rst:464 "This file contains the
  maximum number of memory map areas a process may have."
- Suggested action: accept map_count in {max_maps, max_maps + 1} (and possibly a small arch
  slack), or cite the kernel check in a comment and accept both outcomes.

### testcases/kernel/syscalls/chown/chown04.c  (runtest: syscalls/chown04)
- Category: UNDOC
- Confidence: medium
- Claim under test: chown() fails with EROFS when the named file is on a read-only filesystem.
- Problem: setup() leaves euid=nobody for every case. The EROFS case runs chown("mntpoint", nobody_uid, 0) as nobody on the root-owned mount root of the read-only fs. That also changes the owner of a file the caller does not own, so EPERM applies as well. The kernel returns EROFS only because do_fchownat() calls mnt_want_write() before chown_common()/notify_change(). Neither chown(2) nor POSIX orders the two errors.
- Evidence: chown04.c:48,64,88-95; fs/open.c:849-853 (mnt_want_write before chown_common). chown(2) lists both "EPERM The calling process did not have the required permissions" and "EROFS The named file resides on a read-only filesystem" without precedence.
- Suggested action: Run the EROFS case with euid 0 (as chmod06 does), or chown to (-1, -1) so that only EROFS applies.
- Verification (phase 2, run on real hosts): **CONFIRMED** via RUN,VIRT,READ,GIT. VIRT: chown04 8/8 TPASS. Same creds (euid nobody, egid 0) give EPERM on root-owned tfile_1 (case 1), so for the root-owned ro mount root both EPERM and EROFS apply; EROFS wins only because do_fchownat() calls mnt_want_write() before chown_common() (fs/open.c:849-853). Unchanged since the old-API version (euid nobody for all cases).

### testcases/kernel/syscalls/dup3/dup3_02.c  (runtest: syscalls/dup3_02)
- Category: UNDOC
- Confidence: high (phase 1: medium)
- Claim under test: dup3() returns EINVAL for oldfd == newfd (with and without O_CLOEXEC) and for invalid flags.
- Problem: The test uses hard-coded old_fd = 3 without opening it. The LTP library closes its IPC fd after mmap (lib/tst_test.c:149), so fd 3 is normally not open, and every subcase also meets the EBADF condition ("oldfd isn't an open file descriptor"). The test passes only because ksys_dup3() checks flags and oldfd==newfd before looking up oldfd. dup(2) lists EBADF and both EINVAL conditions without ordering them.
- Evidence: dup3_02.c:22, :29-33; fs/file.c:1429-1442 (EINVAL checks before fd lookup); dup(2) ERRORS lists EBADF/EINVAL with no precedence.
- Suggested action: open a real file in setup and use its fd as oldfd (and a known-valid newfd for the invalid-flags case).
- Verification (phase 2, run on real hosts): **CONFIRMED** via RUN,MUTATION,VIRT. VIRT probe mutant with fd 3 closed (exec 3<&-, as under a normal harness): 'fcntl(3, F_GETFD) = -1 errno=EBADF' yet all 3 cases TPASS with EINVAL, so EBADF also applies and the pass relies on ksys_dup3() checking flags/oldfd==newfd first. Under ltprun fd 3 is the inherited flock fd (/run/lock/ltp-verify.lock): result then depends on the harness's leaked fds.

### testcases/kernel/syscalls/fchmod/fchmod06.c  (runtest: syscalls/fchmod06)
- Category: UNDOC  (secondary: DOCS)
- Confidence: high (phase 1: medium)
- Claim under test: fchmod() fails with EPERM (not owner), EBADF (closed fd), EROFS (read-only fs).
- Problem: setup() switches to euid nobody before all cases run. `mntpoint/file` on the needs_rofs mount is created by root (lib/tst_test.c:1204-1206), so in the EROFS case both EROFS and EPERM apply. The test only passes because chmod_common() calls mnt_want_write() (EROFS) before notify_change()/setattr_prepare() (EPERM); chmod(2) lists both errors without ordering them. Also, the docparse line "EROFS -- file descriptor opened as a read-only" is wrong: EROFS comes from the read-only mount, not from the O_RDONLY fd.
- Evidence: fchmod06.c:35-57; /usr/src/linux/fs/open.c:674-687 (mnt_want_write before notify_change); chmod(2) ERRORS: "EROFS The named file resides on a read-only filesystem."
- Suggested action: run the EROFS case with euid 0 (seteuid only around the EPERM case), and reword the description to "file resides on a read-only filesystem".
- Verification (phase 2, run on real hosts): **CONFIRMED** via RUN,MUTATION,READ. HPE: 3 TPASS. Probe before the EROFS case: 'euid=65534 file st_uid=0 mode=100777', so the EPERM condition (not owner, unprivileged) also holds; EROFS wins only because chmod_common() calls mnt_want_write() before notify_change() (fs/open.c). Docparse 'EROFS -- file descriptor opened as a read-only' is wrong too.

### testcases/kernel/syscalls/fchown/fchown04.c  (runtest: syscalls/fchown04, fchown04_16)
- Category: UNDOC
- Confidence: high (phase 1: medium)
- Claim under test: fchown() fails with EPERM (not owner), EBADF (invalid fd), EROFS (file on read-only fs).

In the EROFS case, chown to (nobody, egid) of a root-owned inode by an unprivileged user also meets the EPERM condition. Probe before EROFS case: 'euid=65534 file st_uid=0' (fd3 = root-owned ro mount root) and the call is fchown(5, 65534, 0) by nobody, so EPERM also applies; EROFS only because vfs_fchown() does mnt_want_write_file() before chown_common() (fs/open.c).

### testcases/kernel/syscalls/fcntl/fcntl11.c  (runtest: syscalls/fcntl11)
- Category: UNDOC
- Confidence: medium
- Claim under test: Region locking: a write lock split/converted by a read lock is reported correctly by F_GETLK from another process.
- Problem: Most probes query a range that overlaps several of the parent's locks (e.g. the whole file `do_test(F_WRLCK,0,0,0)` in blocks 1-8 overlaps both the read and the write lock) and require F_GETLK to return the lowest-offset one. fcntl(2) only promises "details about one of those locks"; POSIX says "Get any lock which blocks". Linux returns the first conflicting entry of inode->flc_posix, which happens to be sorted by start for a single owner because posix_lock_inode() inserts locks in order. That is an implementation detail. The kernel has kept this for decades, so a real failure is unlikely.
- Evidence: fcntl11.c:280-281, 432-433, 477-478, 518-519, 560-561, 598-599; fs/locks.c:1027-1041 (posix_test_lock returns first list match); fcntl(2) "returns details about one of those locks"; POSIX fcntl F_GETLK "Get any lock which blocks ...".
- Suggested action: query ranges that overlap exactly one lock (e.g. probe [0,5) then [10,15)), or document that the test relies on Linux's per-owner sorted lock list.
- Verification (phase 2, run on real hosts): **CONFIRMED** via RUN,READ. HPE: runs clean (blocks 1-9, rc=0; old API reports no TPASS lines). Kernel fs/locks.c posix_test_lock() returns the first conflicting entry of flc_posix, ordered by start only within one owner. Block 1 probe [0,EOF) overlaps RD 1-5 and WR 10-14 and requires 1-5. Reliance on undocumented order confirmed; real failure unlikely.

### testcases/kernel/syscalls/fcntl/fcntl19.c  (runtest: syscalls/fcntl19, fcntl19_64)
- Category: UNDOC
- Confidence: medium
- Claim under test: Unlocking subranges around a write lock leaves the correct remaining lock pieces, as seen by F_GETLK from another process.
- Problem: In block 4 (write lock 10-19, unlock 13-17) the probe `do_test(F_WRLCK, 0, 0, 0)` covers both remaining pieces (10-12 and 18-19) and requires F_GETLK to report 10-12. fcntl(2) only promises "details about one of those locks"; POSIX says "Get any lock which blocks". Linux returns the first entry of the per-inode list (fs/locks.c posix_test_lock), which is sorted only because one owner's locks are inserted in order. The other blocks probe ranges with a single conflicting lock and are fine.
- Evidence: fcntl19.c:459-460; fs/locks.c:1027-1041; fcntl(2) F_GETLK "returns details about one of those locks".
- Suggested action: probe with `do_test(F_WRLCK, 0, 0, 13)` (or start 10, len 3) so only one lock overlaps.
- Verification (phase 2, run on real hosts): **CONFIRMED** via RUN,READ. HPE: runs clean ('Test block N: PASSED', rc=0). Block 4 (:459-460) probes [0,EOF) after unlocking 13-17 of WR 10-19 and requires 10-12 out of two candidate locks; fcntl(2) promises 'one of those locks'. Depends on posix_test_lock() list order (fs/locks.c); other blocks are single-lock probes.

### testcases/kernel/syscalls/fcntl/fcntl21.c  (runtest: syscalls/fcntl21, fcntl21_64)
- Category: UNDOC

Blocks 3-11 probe the whole file (`do_test(F_WRLCK,0,0,0)`) while two locks exist and require the lowest-offset one (e.g. block 3 expects the write lock at 1 rather than the read lock at 10; block 7 expects the read piece at 10). ### testcases/kernel/syscalls/gethostname/gethostname02.c  (runtest: syscalls/gethostname02)
- Category: UNDOC
- Confidence: high (phase 1: medium)
- Claim under test: gethostname() fails with ENAMETOOLONG when len is smaller than the hostname.
- Problem: on most architectures gethostname() is a libc wrapper around uname(2), so this is libc behavior. The man page documents ENAMETOOLONG only for glibc. POSIX says the name is truncated, and musl (a supported LTP libc per doc/users/supported_systems.rst) truncates and returns 0. On musl the test FAILs with no kernel bug. It also FAILs if the hostname is empty (real_length - 1 == -1 becomes a huge size_t).
- Evidence: gethostname02.c:23; gethostname(2) ERRORS: "ENAMETOOLONG (glibc gethostname()) size is smaller than the actual size."; NOTES: "POSIX.1 says that if such truncation occurs, then it is unspecified whether the returned buffer includes a terminating null byte."
- Suggested action: accept success with truncation (0 return) as well, or restrict the check to glibc (`#ifdef __GLIBC__`), and TCONF on an empty hostname.
- Verification (phase 2, run on real hosts): **CONFIRMED** via RUN,CONTAINER. HPE glibc: as-is TPASS ENAMETOOLONG; 1-char hostname (unshare -u) TPASS. Empty hostname in a UTS ns: real_length-1 -> SIZE_MAX, glibc fortify aborts '*** buffer overflow detected ***: terminated' (crash, not TFAIL). musl truncation part not testable here; gethostname(2) documents ENAMETOOLONG for glibc only.
- Verification (phase 3, glibc vs musl build and libc sources): **CONFIRMED** via BULK,MUSL,RUN,SRC. [m01: CONFIRMED] HPE glibc: 'TPASS: len is smaller than the actual size : ENAMETOOLONG (36)'; musl: 'gethostname02.c:24: TFAIL: len is smaller than the actual size succeeded'. musl src/unistd/gethostname.c:9-12 truncates and returns 0 (POSIX-allowed); glibc sysdeps/posix/gethostname.c:40 sets ENAMETOOLONG. Test is glibc-specific || [m09: UNCHANGED] HPE glibc: PASS; musl: 'TFAIL: len is smaller than the actual size succeeded' (rc 1). Same as m01 record (CONFIRMED UNDOC high: musl src/unistd/gethostname.c:9-12 truncates, POSIX-allowed); nothing new

### testcases/kernel/syscalls/io_cancel/io_cancel01.c  (runtest: syscalls/io_cancel01)
- Category: UNDOC
- Confidence: medium
- Claim under test: io_cancel() with an invalid pointer returns EFAULT.
- Problem: The call is io_cancel(ctx=0, iocb=NULL, result=NULL). ctx 0 is also an invalid
  AIO context, for which io_cancel(2) documents EINVAL. The test requires EFAULT, which only
  holds because the kernel dereferences iocb->aio_key before lookup_ioctx(). The man page does
  not order these errors. Using a valid ctx (io_setup) would make EFAULT the only correct outcome.
- Evidence: io_cancel01.c:23-24; /usr/src/linux/fs/aio.c:2238-2245 (get_user(iocb) before
  lookup_ioctx); io_cancel(2) ERRORS: "EFAULT One of the data structures points to invalid data."
  / "EINVAL The AIO context specified by ctx_id is invalid."
- Suggested action: set up a valid context with io_setup() before calling io_cancel with NULL
  iocb, or accept EINVAL as well.
- Verification (phase 2, run on real hosts): **CONFIRMED** via RUN,MUTATION. HPE: as-is TPASS EFAULT. Work copy adds probes: io_cancel(ctx=0, valid iocb ptr) -> EINVAL; io_cancel(valid io_setup ctx, NULL, NULL) -> EFAULT. Both errors apply to the original call; EFAULT wins only because fs/aio.c:2238 get_user(iocb->aio_key) precedes lookup_ioctx(). Valid ctx makes EFAULT unambiguous.

### testcases/kernel/syscalls/keyctl/keyctl17.c  (runtest: syscalls/keyctl17)
- Category: UNDOC
- Confidence: medium
- Claim under test: KEYCTL_GET_SECURITY on a key without View permission fails with ENOKEY.
- Problem: The documented permission error is EACCES ("The caller must have view permission"; keyctl(2) ERRORS: "EACCES The requested operation wasn't permitted"). ENOKEY only comes out because the kernel, after getting -EACCES, tries key_get_instantiation_authkey() and returns that lookup's error instead of the original EACCES. That is an implementation artifact; a kernel change to propagate EACCES would be reasonable and would fail this test.
- Evidence: keyctl17.c:30; security/keys/keyctl.c:1582-1591; KEYCTL_GET_SECURITY(2const) "The caller must have view permission on the specified key."
- Suggested action: Accept both EACCES and ENOKEY (TST_EXP_FAIL_ARR) for the no-View case.
- Verification (phase 2, run on real hosts): **CONFIRMED** via RUN,READ,GIT. HPE: both cases TPASS ENOKEY. keyctl.c:1582-1591: -EACCES from lookup_user_key is replaced by key_get_instantiation_authkey()'s error (ENOKEY). Commit 4b8e26706d10 and test header admit it is the auth-token fallback; man page only says view permission is needed. Accept EACCES too.

- Confidence: low
- Claim under test: lchown() fails with EROFS when the file is on a read-only filesystem.
- Problem: The process runs as "nobody" (seteuid in setup) and chowns the root-owned root directory of the read-only mount. Both EROFS and EPERM ("process not owner") apply. The test passes only because do_fchownat() calls mnt_want_write() before chown_common(). lchown(2) does not order these errors. This is a minor robustness issue, since the kernel order has been stable for a long time.
- Evidence: lchown02.c:62, 80-89; fs/open.c:851-853 (mnt_want_write before chown_common).
- Suggested action: Run the EROFS case as root (seteuid(0) around it), or chown to the file's current owner, so that only EROFS can apply.
- Verification (phase 2, run on real hosts): **CONFIRMED** via RUN,READ. HPE: lchown02 8/8 TPASS incl. 'Read-only filesystem: EROFS'; fs/open.c do_fchownat() calls mnt_want_write() (l.851) before chown_common() (l.853), so EROFS wins over EPERM for nobody chowning root-owned dir; lchown(2) gives no order. Reasoning holds; kernel order is long-stable so keep low.

### testcases/kernel/syscalls/mmap/mmap08.c  (runtest: syscalls/mmap08)
- Category: UNDOC
- Confidence: medium
- Claim under test: mmap() fails with EBADF when the fd is not a valid descriptor.
- Problem: `page_sz` is a static that is never assigned, so the call is
  mmap(NULL, 0, PROT_WRITE, MAP_SHARED, -1, 0). (SAFE_CLOSE in setup sets fd to -1.) Length 0
  is a separate documented EINVAL condition, so the call has two errors at once. The test
  passes only because ksys_mmap_pgoff() does fget(fd) before do_mmap() checks `!len`.
  mmap(2) does not order these errors.
- Evidence: mmap08.c:17, 28-29 (page_sz never set); mm/mmap.c ksys_mmap_pgoff(): `file =
  fget(fd); if (!file) return -EBADF;` comes before vm_mmap_pgoff() -> do_mmap()
  `if (!len) return -EINVAL;`. mmap(2) ERRORS: "EINVAL (since Linux 2.6.12) length was 0."
- Suggested action: set page_sz = getpagesize() in setup.
- Verification (phase 2, run on real hosts): **CONFIRMED** via RUN,VIRT,READ,GIT. VIRT as-is TPASS EBADF; call is mmap(NULL, 0, ..., fd=-1) because page_sz is never assigned. git: rewrite bff113e57ffa dropped 'page_sz = getpagesize()' from setup. ksys_mmap_pgoff() fget(fd)->EBADF (mm/mmap.c l.590-592) precedes do_mmap() '!len' EINVAL. Fix: set page_sz in setup.

### testcases/open_posix_testsuite/conformance/definitions/pthread_h/6-1-buildonly.c  (openposix: conformance/definitions/pthread_h/6-1-buildonly)
- Category: UNDOC (phase 1: UNDEF)
- Confidence: medium (phase 1: low)
- Claim under test: pthread_self() is declared as `pthread_t pthread_self(void)`.
- Problem: The check does `if (ptid == 0)`. POSIX pthread_t is opaque and may be a structure
  (POSIX pthread.h rationale gives a struct example; PTHREAD_NULL was added for this reason), so
  the compile check depends on an arithmetic pthread_t that POSIX does not require. Harmless on
  glibc/musl, but on a conforming implementation with a struct pthread_t it reports a compile
  failure that is not a conformance bug.
- Evidence: pthread_h/6-1-buildonly.c; https://pubs.opengroup.org/onlinepubs/9799919799/basedefs/pthread.h.html
  RATIONALE "Since pthread_t is an opaque type, a definition of PTHREAD_NULL was added."
- Suggested action: drop the comparison (e.g. `(void)ptid;`) or use pthread_equal().
- Verification (phase 2, run on real hosts): **REVISED** via BUILD,READ. Compiles on glibc (pthread_t=unsigned long). POSIX XBD sys/types.h: all types arithmetic 'with the following exceptions' incl. pthread_t (Issue 6 TC added it so it may be a struct). A struct-typed copy (my_pthread_t ptid; if (ptid == 0)) -> gcc 'error: invalid operands to binary =='. Not C UB: impl-defined type dependence -> UNDOC.
- Verification conclusion: Phase-1 reasoning holds, but it is not C undefined behaviour: on an implementation with a struct pthread_t the comparison is a compile error. That is reliance on implementation-defined representation -> UNDOC. Action unchanged: drop `ptid == 0` (use `(void)ptid;`).
- Verification (phase 3, glibc vs musl build and libc sources): **CONFIRMED** via BUILD,MUSL,SRC. glibc and musl logfile.conformance-all: 'pthread_h/6-1-buildonly compile PASSED' under both. pthread_t: glibc pthreadtypes.h:27 unsigned long; musl alltypes.h.in:53-57 'struct __pthread *' in C (unsigned long only for C++) -> ptid==0 compiles on musl only as a null-pointer compare: a third representation, confirming the check depends on the impl-defined type


## UNDEF: Tests undefined or unspecified behavior

Documentation explicitly leaves the outcome open (unspecified, implementation-defined, 'may fail'), or the test itself invokes C undefined behavior, yet the test requires one specific result. Action: drop the subcase, or reduce it to 'any documented outcome, no crash'.

116 testcases. Sorted by path; confidence shown in each entry.

### testcases/kernel/controllers/cpuctl/cpuctl_latency_check_task.c  (helper for run_cpuctl_latency_test.sh)
- Category: UNDEF  (secondary: FRAGILE)
- Confidence: high (phase 1: medium)
- Claim under test: measures usleep() overshoot over 201 iterations and FAILs if any single overshoot is above ALLOWED.
- Problem: `actual_us = cur.tv_usec - prev.tv_usec` is unsigned, so it wraps to about 4.29e9 whenever the sleep crosses a second boundary. With sleeps of up to 200ms, almost every run crosses one. `actual = 1e6*actual_s + actual_us` then converts a double greater than UINT_MAX to unsigned int, which is undefined behavior in C. On x86-64 it truncates to the right value by luck. On arm64, fcvtzu saturates to UINT_MAX, so delta becomes huge and the result is a spurious FAIL. A single sample above a fixed threshold under 100 hogs is also flaky. The result is never propagated (see the script entry above).
- Evidence: cpuctl_latency_check_task.c:120-128.
- Suggested action: compute with timespec and signed 64-bit arithmetic (or use tst_timer), or drop together with the script.
- Verification (phase 2, run on real hosts): **CONFIRMED** via READ,BUILD,RUN. Extracted the delta arithmetic (cpuctl_latency_check_task.c:120-123) into ub.c; prev=5.950000 cur=6.050000: actual_us=4294067296, 1e6*actual_s+actual_us=4295067296.0 > UINT_MAX; x86-64 -O2 gives actual=100000 by luck; same code with -fsanitize=float-cast-overflow -fsanitize-trap=all dies with SIGILL (rc 132) -> UB confirmed. Helper never runs on v2 hosts (test_controllers.sh TCONFs)

### testcases/kernel/io/direct_io/diotest4.c  (runtest: dio/dio04, dio10)
- Category: UNDEF  (secondary: FRAGILE)
- Confidence: high
- Claim under test: O_DIRECT error conditions, including "[3] odd count" (count=1) and "[14] non-aligned buffer" (buf+1), both required to fail with EINVAL.
- Problem: open(2) explicitly leaves misaligned O_DIRECT handling to the filesystem: they "can either fail with EINVAL or fall back to buffered I/O". The test hard-codes a whitelist (NFS, btrfs, FUSE, tmpfs) and otherwise requires EINVAL. Other in-tree filesystems legitimately fall back: ext4 returns dio_align 0 for data=journal/inline data/verity inodes and fs-block alignment for fscrypt inodes, so ext4_should_use_dio() picks buffered I/O; f2fs falls back for I/O that is logical-block but not fs-block aligned. On those, read/write succeed and the test TFAILs.
- Evidence: diotest4.c:252-264, :144-157 (fs-type whitelist + runtest_f EINVAL); open(2) O_DIRECT: "In Linux alignment restrictions vary by filesystem and kernel version and might be absent entirely. The handling of misaligned O_DIRECT I/Os also varies; they can either fail with EINVAL or fall back to buffered I/O."; /usr/src/linux/fs/ext4/file.c:55-67 ext4_should_use_dio(); /usr/src/linux/fs/f2fs/file.c:5112-5140 f2fs_should_use_dio().
- Suggested action: query statx(STATX_DIOALIGN) (Linux 6.1+) and accept either EINVAL or a successful (buffered fallback) transfer for misaligned I/O; TCONF only when the alignment is unknown.

### testcases/kernel/lib/numa_cpuset.c  (helper; used by mem/ksm/ksm02, ksm04, mem/oom/oom04, oom05)
- Category: UNDEF
- Confidence: high (phase 1: medium)
- Claim under test: helper write_node_cpusets() sets cpuset.mems to node `nd` and cpuset.cpus to that node's online CPUs, falling back to CPU0 for CPU-less nodes.
- Problem: gather_node_cpus() unconditionally strips the trailing comma with `cpus[strlen(cpus) - 1] = '\0'`. When the node has no (online) CPUs, `cpus` is empty, `strlen()-1` wraps to SIZE_MAX and the store lands one byte before the stack buffer (C out-of-bounds write, UB). This is precisely the memory-only-node case (CXL/PMEM/HBM nodes, or all node CPUs offlined) that write_node_cpusets() explicitly tries to support with its "No CPUs in the node" branch. oom04/oom05 pick the node via get_allowed_nodes(NH_MEMS), which does not filter CPU-less nodes, so they can hit it.
- Evidence: numa_cpuset.c:41-42 (strip), 56-63 (empty-case fallback); oom/oom04.c:58-62.
- Suggested action: guard the strip with `if (cpus[0])` (or `size_t l = strlen(cpus); if (l) cpus[l-1] = '\0';`).
- Verification (phase 2, run on real hosts): **CONFIRMED** via BUILD,RUN,READ. HPE: harness #including numa_cpuset.c with a canary byte placed right before cpus[]; gather_node_cpus(cpus, 7) (node with no CPUs) overwrote the canary 0x43->0x00 (cpus[strlen-1] with strlen 0); node0 call leaves canary intact -> out-of-bounds write confirmed

### testcases/kernel/syscalls/brk/brk01.c  (runtest: syscalls/brk01)
- Category: UNDEF
- Confidence: high (phase 1: medium)
- Claim under test: brk() can grow, keep and shrink the program break, and the new heap memory is writable.
- Problem: After growing, the test writes to `*(char *)cur_brk`, the byte at the new break. That byte is one past the end of the data segment. It is only mapped because the kernel rounds the heap VMA up to a page boundary. inc is 2*pagesize-1, so if the starting break is at page offset 1, the new break is page-aligned and the write lands outside the heap VMA, giving SIGSEGV (or it silently hits whatever is mapped next). Usually the starting break is page-aligned and the write lands in the padding, so the test passes by luck. Either way the test does not check that the allocated range itself is writable.
- Evidence: brk01.c:17,41,66-67; mm/mmap.c:155-156 (the heap VMA ends at PAGE_ALIGN(brk)).
- Suggested action: Write to `(char *)cur_brk - 1`, or to the whole range [old_brk, new_brk).
- Verification (phase 2, run on real hosts): **CONFIRMED** via RUN,MUTATION,VIRT. VIRT: brk01 3/3 TPASS as-is. Mutant that first moves the break to page offset 1 (brk(sbrk(0)+pagesize-off+1)), so that cur+2*ps-1 is page aligned: 'MUT: start break 0x1de61001' then 'TBROK: Test killed by SIGSEGV!' -> the write at *(char*)cur_brk is one byte past the heap and only works thanks to page rounding.
