### testcases/kernel/syscalls/epoll_wait/epoll_wait16.c  (runtest: syscalls/epoll_wait16)
- Category: UNDEF
- Confidence: high
- Claim under test: with EPOLLEXCLUSIVE, one event on the target fd wakes exactly one of several
  waiting epoll instances.
- Problem: epoll_ctl(2) only promises "one or more" epoll fds receive an event; "exactly one" is
  current kernel behaviour (__wake_up_common with nr_exclusive=1 stops at the first
  ep_poll_callback returning ewake=1), not a documented guarantee. ep_poll_callback returns
  ewake=0 for an instance whose ep->wq has no waiter, so the walk continues to the next entry;
  the documentation deliberately leaves room for more than one wakeup. The test FAILs if
  nwoken != round+1.
- Evidence: epoll_wait16.c:12-13, :96-101; epoll_ctl(2) EPOLLEXCLUSIVE: "one or more of the epoll
  file descriptors will receive an event with epoll_wait(2)"; /usr/src/linux/fs/eventpoll.c
  ep_poll_callback (line ~1491, ewake logic).
- Suggested action: Relax to "fewer than NWAITERS woken per event" (i.e. not all, thundering herd
  avoided) or "at least one", or document that the test checks current kernel behaviour.

### testcases/kernel/syscalls/fpathconf/fpathconf01.c  (runtest: syscalls/fpathconf01)
- Category: UNDEF  (secondary: DOCS)
- Confidence: low (phase 1: medium)
- Claim under test: "basic functionality of the fpathconf(2) system call".
- Problem: All nine names are queried on a regular file, and every call must return >= 0
  (TST_EXP_POSITIVE). The docs do not require that for most of these names on a regular file:
  - fpathconf(3) says _PC_MAX_CANON, _PC_MAX_INPUT and _PC_VDISABLE need fd to refer to a terminal.
  - POSIX (notes 2, 3/4 and 6 in the fpathconf table) leaves it unspecified whether
    MAX_CANON/MAX_INPUT/VDISABLE (non-terminal), NAME_MAX/PATH_MAX/NO_TRUNC (non-directory) and
    PIPE_BUF (not a pipe/FIFO/directory) are supported. EINVAL is an allowed error for an
    unsupported association.
  - fpathconf(3) also allows -1 with errno unchanged for an indeterminate limit or an unsupported
    option, and the test treats that as a failure.
  pathconf01 was just relaxed for the same reason (commit 5b5bab8c18a7). Also, fpathconf is a
  libc function, not a syscall.
- Evidence: fpathconf01.c:17-25, 34, 39; fpathconf(3): "_PC_MAX_CANON ... where fd or path must refer
  to a terminal", ERRORS "EINVAL The implementation does not support an association of name with the
  specified file", RETURN VALUE "-1 is returned and errno is not changed"; POSIX
  https://pubs.opengroup.org/onlinepubs/9799919799/functions/fpathconf.html notes 2/3/6.
- Suggested action: Do as pathconf01 now does: accept EINVAL (TCONF) for the unspecified names, or
  use a directory fd for NAME_MAX/PATH_MAX/NO_TRUNC/PIPE_BUF and a pty for the terminal names. Accept
  -1 with errno 0. Fix "system call" in the description.
- Verification (phase 2, run on real hosts): **REVISED** via RUN,READ,GIT. HPE glibc: 9/9 TPASS (255,255,0,65535,255,4096,4096,1,1) on a regular file. POSIX notes allow EINVAL for these names on a non-terminal/non-dir fd, so the reasoning holds, but glibc/musl/bionic all return constants here (unlike pathconf01's _PC_REC_* that broke Bionic, git 5b5bab8c18a7); no known libc fails -> low.
- Verification conclusion: The POSIX argument is right (MAX_CANON/MAX_INPUT/VDISABLE on a non-terminal, NAME_MAX/PATH_MAX/NO_TRUNC/PIPE_BUF on a regular file are "unspecified", EINVAL allowed), but all of the names fpathconf01 queries are answered with constants by glibc and, as far as known, musl and Bionic, so no supported libc fails today. Keep the suggested relaxation (TCONF on EINVAL, "libc function" in the description) but at low confidence.
- Verification (phase 3, glibc vs musl build and libc sources): **CONFIRMED** via MUSL,RUN,SRC. HPE glibc: 9/9 TPASS (LINK_MAX 65535 via statfs, linux/fpathconf.c:37); musl: 9/9 TPASS (LINK_MAX 8). musl src/conf/fpathconf.c:7-34 is a constant table that ignores fd (probe fpathconf(-1,_PC_NAME_MAX)=255 errno 0; glibc EBADF). No libc returns EINVAL for these names, so low stays; under musl the test touches no kernel at all

### testcases/kernel/syscalls/getgroups/getgroups01.c  (runtest: syscalls/getgroups01, getgroups01_16)
- Category: UNDEF
- Confidence: high (phase 1: medium)
- Claim under test: item 4, "getgroups() succeeds and gidset contains group id returned from getgid()".
- Problem: the kernel returns exactly the list that was last passed to setgroups(). It never adds the (e)gid. getgroups(2) explicitly leaves this unspecified. setup() calls setgroups(3, {0,1,2}) but ignores the result, and the test has no needs_root. As root the check passes only because gid 0 happens to be in that list. As non-root, setgroups fails silently and the check depends on how the login/launcher built the group list. Running under `sg`, under a systemd unit with `Group=`, or in a container with a minimal group list gives a false FAIL.
- Evidence: getgroups01.c:154-171, :187-188; getgroups(2): "It is unspecified whether the effective group ID of the calling process is included in the returned list."; kernel/groups.c getgroups copies current_cred()->group_info verbatim.
- Suggested action: set needs_root, use SAFE_SETGROUPS with a known list and compare against that list, or drop item 4.
- Verification (phase 2, run on real hosts): **CONFIRMED** via RUN,READ. HPE as root: as-is item 4 TPASS only because setgroups({0,1,2}) contains gid 0. 'setpriv --regid 10 --keep-groups getgroups01' -> item 4 'TFAIL: getgroups(NGROUPS,gidset) ret 3, does not contain gid 10 (from getgid)'; getgroups(2) leaves egid inclusion unspecified.

### testcases/kernel/syscalls/listxattr/listxattr01.c  (runtest: syscalls/listxattr01)
- Category: UNDEF
- Confidence: low
- Claim under test: listxattr() returns the security.ltptest1 name.
- Problem: has_attribute() is called with llen = sizeof(buf) (64) instead of the returned length TST_RET. buf is an uninitialized stack array, so the scan reads indeterminate bytes past the returned list, and strlen() on that garbage can run past the end of buf. For the positive check this can almost never cause a false result, but the code is UB.
- Evidence: listxattr01.c:47-55.
- Suggested action: Pass TST_RET as the length (or zero buf first).
- Verification (phase 2, run on real hosts): **CONFIRMED** via RUN,MUTATION,VIRT. VIRT as-is TPASS. Mutant: setxattr of security.ltptest1 disabled, buf zeroed and 'security.ltptest1' planted at buf+44 before the call -> 'V07: listxattr returned 17' (only security.selinux) yet 'TPASS: listxattr() succeeded': has_attribute() scans sizeof(buf)=64 not TST_RET. Real stack garbage rarely matches, so keep low.

### testcases/kernel/syscalls/llistxattr/llistxattr01.c  (runtest: syscalls/llistxattr01)
- Category: UNDEF

### testcases/kernel/syscalls/tgkill/tgkill01.c  (runtest: syscalls/tgkill01)
- Category: UNDEF
- Confidence: low
- Claim under test: tgkill() delivers SIGUSR1 to the specified thread.
- Problem: `sigusr1_thread` is a plain (non-volatile, non-atomic) `pthread_t` global. It is written by the signal handler running on another thread and busy-polled by the main thread (`while (pthread_equal(sigusr1_thread, pthread_self())) usleep(1000);`). That is a C11 data race (UB). In practice the opaque usleep()/pthread_equal() calls force a reload, so it works with current compilers, but nothing guarantees it (e.g. under LTO with an inlined pthread_equal).
- Evidence: tgkill01.c:27-32, 82-91
- Suggested action: Record the delivering thread's index or tid in a `volatile sig_atomic_t`/`_Atomic` variable (or use `__atomic_load_n`/`__atomic_store_n`).
- Verification (phase 2, run on real hosts): **UNCHANGED** via RUN,REPEAT,READ. HPE: TPASS, 5 runs x -i 20 all pass. objdump of installed binary: pthread_equal inlined (0 calls), loop is 'call usleep; mov sigusr1_thread(%rip),%rax; cmp; je loop', so the global is reloaded only because usleep() is an opaque call. Data race is real per C11 but cannot be shown to break with the current toolchain

### testcases/network/nfs/nfslock01/nfs_flock_dgen.c  (runtest: helper of net.nfs/nfslock01_*)
- Category: UNDEF
- Confidence: high (phase 1: medium)
- Claim under test: generates a file of nlines x nchars bytes.
- Problem: `char buf[BUFSIZ]` is an uninitialised local array. The loop fills only buf[0..nchars-2], and then `fprintf(fp, "%s\n", buf)` reads until a NUL byte. Correct output depends on buf[nchars-1] happening to be 0 (fresh stack pages), which is undefined behaviour. - Evidence: nfs_flock_dgen.c:19 (buf), 55-56 (fill loop), 58 (fprintf "%s\n").
- Suggested action: Set `buf[nchars - 1] = '\0'` (or use fwrite of nchars-1 bytes plus '\n') and check fopen.
- Verification (phase 2, run on real hosts): **CONFIRMED** via BUILD,RUN. local: gcc -O2 build, dgen 64x1000 -> 64000 bytes (stack happened to be 0); same source with -ftrivial-auto-var-init=pattern -> 8193000 bytes, lines run into 0xFE bytes past buf[nchars-1] -> nfslock01 size check would TBROK; correctness depends on uninitialised stack

### testcases/open_posix_testsuite/conformance/definitions/mqueue_h/1-1.c  (openposix: conformance/definitions/mqueue_h/1-1)
- Category: UNDEF

  long arithmetic, which is signed overflow (C UB; gcc warns "integer overflow in expression").

  wraparound of a UB expression. The first check (`x = -LONG_MIN; x != -LONG_MIN`) compares
  the overflowed expression with itself. Works today with gcc constant folding, but the
  verification is based on UB rather than on the type.
- Evidence: mqueue_h/1-1.c TEST_LIMITS macro; POSIX mqueue.h: "long mq_flags ... long mq_curmsgs".
- Suggested action: replace with a compile-time type check, e.g.
  `_Static_assert(_Generic(mqs.mq_flags, long: 1, default: 0), ...)` or sizeof + assignment of
  LONG_MAX/LONG_MIN without overflowing expressions.
- Verification (phase 2, run on real hosts): **CONFIRMED** via BUILD,RUN. HPE: mqueue_h_1-1.run-test PASSED rc=0. gcc -Wall: 12x '-Woverflow: integer overflow in expression ... of type long int' (lines 17,18,31 x4 fields): -LONG_MIN and LONG_MAX+1 are overflowing constant expressions (C11 6.6p4 constraint, UB); result relies on gcc's wraparound folding. UBSan not available on hosts (no libubsan).

### testcases/open_posix_testsuite/conformance/interfaces/aio_cancel/2-1.c  (openposix: conformance/interfaces/aio_cancel/2-1)
- Category: UNDEF
- Confidence: low
- Claim under test: aio_cancel(fd, NULL) cancels all outstanding cancelable requests.
- Problem: Requires aio_error()==ECANCELED for queued writes 3..7. POSIX lets the implementation decide which operations are cancelable, so a conforming implementation could cancel none of them (and return AIO_NOTCANCELED). The test encodes the glibc model: one worker per fd, queued requests cancelable, running ones not. This holds on Linux/glibc and is stable, so the risk is portability (musl, other libcs), not false FAILs on glibc.
- Evidence: aio_cancel/2-1.c:82-91; https://pubs.opengroup.org/onlinepubs/9799919799/functions/aio_cancel.html: "Which operations are cancelable is implementation-defined."
- Suggested action: Document the glibc dependency in the test header, or turn the per-request ECANCELED check into TCONF/UNTESTED when aio_cancel() returns AIO_NOTCANCELED for everything.
- Verification (phase 2, run on real hosts): **CONFIRMED** via RUN,READ. HPE: Test PASSED as-is (glibc: queued requests cancelable). Code :82-91 requires ECANCELED for every request after the blocked one; POSIX: which ops are cancelable is implementation-defined. No false FAIL possible on glibc; portability-only, low stands
- Verification (phase 3, glibc vs musl build and libc sources): **UNCHANGED** via MUSL,RUN,SRC,READ. HPE glibc: Test PASSED; musl: hangs in aio_cancel, rc=137. musl src/aio/aio.c:382-392 aio_cancel holds q->lock while waiting for each cancelled worker; a queued worker sits in pthread_cond_wait (aio.c:254), which relocks q->lock before acting on cancel (thread/pthread_cond_timedwait.c:145,168) -> deadlock (musl bug). musl also cancels queued writes, so both libcs fit the test's model

### testcases/open_posix_testsuite/conformance/interfaces/aio_cancel/5-1.c  (openposix: conformance/interfaces/aio_cancel/5-1)
- Category: UNDEF  (secondary: FRAGILE)
- Confidence: high (phase 1: medium)
- Claim under test: An aiocb that was not cancelled is not modified.
- Problem: (1) The test requires aio_cancel() to return AIO_NOTCANCELED and the blocked write to stay EINPROGRESS. That only holds if in-progress operations are non-cancelable, which POSIX leaves implementation-defined. musl, for example, cancels the worker thread, which is blocked in a cancellation point (send). (2) Synchronization: it polls until task #1 reports done, then relies on one 10 ms nanosleep for glibc's worker to dequeue task #2 and start the blocking send. In glibc, the error status is published before the next request is marked running, so under heavy load task #2 can still be queued. It then gets cancelled, aio_cancel() returns AIO_CANCELED, and the test FAILs.
- Evidence: aio_cancel/5-1.c:73-102 (the nanosleep at :76 is the only grace period); POSIX aio_cancel "Which operations are cancelable is implementation-defined."
- Suggested action: Document the glibc dependency. Wait until task #2 is observably blocked (e.g. poll that the receiver socket holds 2 messages and give extra margin), or accept AIO_CANCELED with TCONF/UNRESOLVED when the blocked task was cancelled.
- Verification (phase 2, run on real hosts): **REVISED** via RUN,REPEAT,STRESS,VIRT,READ. No FAIL in 140 runs (HPE 50 + 50 ltpstress, VIRT 20 + 20 stress). glibc rt/aio_misc.c handle_fildes_io: error status of #1 set, #2 dequeued and marked running=allocated in ONE hold of __aio_requests_mutex; aio_cancel takes that mutex and treats 'allocated' as AIO_NOTCANCELED -> 10 ms race cannot occur on glibc. UNDEF only
- Verification conclusion: The FRAGILE part (task #2 still queued after the 10 ms grace period) cannot happen with glibc. Once aio_error(#1) is no longer EINPROGRESS, #2 is already "allocated" under the same lock that aio_cancel needs. What remains is the portability point (implementation-defined cancelability, e.g. musl), so drop the secondary FRAGILE, use low, and limit the action to documenting the glibc dependency.
- Verification (phase 3, glibc vs musl build and libc sources): **CONFIRMED** via MUSL,RUN,SRC. HPE glibc: Test PASSED; musl: hangs in aio_cancel(), rc=137 (musl deadlock, see 2-1). Probe with 1 write blocked in progress on full DGRAM socket: glibc aio_cancel=AIO_NOTCANCELED, EINPROGRESS (rt/aio_cancel.c:90-92); musl AIO_CANCELED, ECANCELED (aio.c:385-388 pthread_cancel) -> 5-1 would FAIL on musl

- Category: UNDEF

### testcases/open_posix_testsuite/conformance/interfaces/lio_listio/14-1.c  (openposix: conformance/interfaces/lio_listio/14-1)
- Category: UNDEF
- Confidence: medium
- Claim under test: failure of an individual request does not prevent completion of the others.
- Problem: the failing request is an aiocb with aio_fildes = -1 submitted with LIO_NOWAIT, and the test FAILs unless lio_listio() returns 0. POSIX lets EBADF be detected synchronously at submission; an implementation that does so does not queue that request and lio_listio() then returns -1 with errno EIO. Both behaviours are conforming, but only the asynchronous one passes. glibc detects it asynchronously, so Linux/glibc passes. The test also never checks that request 2 actually failed.
- Evidence: lio_listio/14-1.c:107-108, :141-151; POSIX aio_write(): "Each of the following conditions may be detected synchronously at the time of the call to aio_write(), or asynchronously." [EBADF]; lio_listio() ERRORS: "[EIO] One or more of the individual I/O operations failed."
- Suggested action: accept ret == -1 && errno == EIO as well (then check aio_error() of the good requests), and verify aio_error(aiocbs[2]) == EBADF.
- Verification (phase 2, run on real hosts): **CONFIRMED** via RUN,MUTATION,READ. HPE as-is PASS (glibc reports bad-fd request asynchronously). Mutation: request #2 given the valid fd (nothing fails) -> still 'lio_listio/14-1.c PASSED' rc=0: test never verifies that request 2 failed. Sync-detection (-1/EIO) rejection is from code :141-151; not testable on glibc
- Verification (phase 3, glibc vs musl build and libc sources): **REVISED** via MUSL,RUN,REPEAT,SRC,READ. HPE glibc: PASSED; musl: FAIL 2/2 'Error lio_listio() Resource temporarily unavailable'. musl lio_listio.c:89-104 stops at the first failing submit (sync EBADF on #2), never queues #3..#9 and returns EAGAIN, which breaks assertion 14 itself -> musl bug, true FAIL. The sync-detection concern holds; the suggested fix must also catch this
- Verification conclusion: musl does detect the bad fd synchronously, as the finding anticipated. But musl's lio_listio stops at the first failed submit (lio_listio.c:89-104): requests #3..#9 are never queued, and it returns -1/EAGAIN, not EIO. That violates the assertion under test ("failure of an individual request does not prevent completion of any other"), so the musl FAIL is a true positive (musl bug). The finding holds for a conforming sync-detecting libc. Corrected action: accept -1/EIO only if the other 9 requests were still queued and complete; check aio_return()==BUF_SIZE for them (the :175 check uses '&&', so a never-queued zeroed aiocb with err 0 passes; use '||'); and verify aio_error(aiocbs[2])==EBADF.

### testcases/open_posix_testsuite/conformance/interfaces/lio_listio/9-1.c  (openposix: conformance/interfaces/lio_listio/9-1)
- Category: UNDEF
- Confidence: low
- Claim under test: LIO_WRITE submits the entry as if by aio_write().
- Problem: after the asynchronous write at aio_offset 0, the test reads the data back with plain read() at the current file offset. POSIX says that offset is unspecified once an aio operation has been enqueued. glibc uses pwrite and leaves the offset at 0, so Linux passes. An implementation that advances the offset makes read() return 0, and the test reports UNRESOLVED.
- Evidence: lio_listio/9-1.c:101; POSIX aio_write(): "After a successful call to enqueue an asynchronous I/O operation, the value of the file offset for the file is unspecified."
- Suggested action: use pread(fd, check, BUF_SIZE, 0) or lseek(fd, 0, SEEK_SET) first.
- Verification (phase 2, run on real hosts): **CONFIRMED** via RUN,MUTATION. HPE as-is PASS (glibc uses pwrite, offset stays 0). Mutation simulating an impl that advances the offset (lseek(fd, BUF_SIZE) after lio_listio) -> rc=2 'Error at read(): No such file or directory' (UNRESOLVED, stale errno). Mechanism holds; no false result on glibc
- Verification (phase 3, glibc vs musl build and libc sources): **UNCHANGED** via MUSL,RUN,SRC. HPE glibc: Test PASSED; musl: Test PASSED. Both use pwrite for a non-O_APPEND regular file, so the offset stays 0: musl aio.c:262 (append ? write : pwrite), glibc rt/aio_misc.c:563-569. The file offset is unspecified only per POSIX; no Linux libc moves it

### testcases/open_posix_testsuite/conformance/interfaces/pthread_attr_destroy/1-1.c  (openposix: conformance/interfaces/pthread_attr_destroy/1-1)
- Category: UNDEF  (secondary: WEAK)
- Confidence: high (phase 1: medium)
- Claim under test: after pthread_attr_destroy, pthread_create with that attr returns EINVAL.
- Problem: POSIX makes any use of a destroyed attributes object undefined behaviour, and the header comment quoted in 2-1.c says the same. The test accepts EINVAL or 0 as PASS (glibc returns 0) and fails on any other error code, even though UB permits any outcome (another errno, a crash). The assertion has no defined expected result, so the test checks nothing portable.
- Evidence: 1-1.c: `ret = pthread_create(&new_th, &new_attr, ...)` after destroy; POSIX pthread_attr_destroy: "the results of otherwise referencing the object after it has been destroyed are undefined."
- Suggested action: Drop the test, or reduce it to "pthread_attr_destroy returns 0" (already covered by 3-1).
- Verification (phase 2, run on real hosts): **CONFIRMED** via RUN,READ,GIT. HPE: PASS 'Though returned 0 when creating a thread with a destroyed attribute...' (glibc returns 0). Code FAILs on any errno other than EINVAL/EPERM/EAGAIN/0. POSIX pthread_attr_destroy (2024 text, fetched): 'results of otherwise referencing the object after it has been destroyed are undefined'; Issue 7 removed EINVAL.
- Verification (phase 3, glibc vs musl build and libc sources): **CONFIRMED** via MUSL,RUN,SRC. HPE glibc: PASS 'returned 0 ... destroyed attribute'; musl: same PASS. musl pthread_attr_destroy.c:3-6 is a no-op; glibc nptl/pthread_attr_destroy.c frees iattr->extension (cpuset) so reuse of a destroyed attr with affinity would read freed memory. No libc returns the EINVAL the header asserts; UB as stated.

### testcases/open_posix_testsuite/conformance/interfaces/pthread_attr_setdetachstate/2-1.c  (openposix: conformance/interfaces/pthread_attr_setdetachstate/2-1)
- Category: UNDEF
- Confidence: high
- Claim under test: pthread_join() and pthread_detach() on a thread created detached return an error (EINVAL is required).
- Problem: Since POSIX.1-2008, passing a non-joinable thread to pthread_join/pthread_detach is undefined behaviour, and the EINVAL error was removed. The thread may also already have exited (it only calls pthread_exit), which ends the lifetime of its ID, a second source of UB. glibc happens to return EINVAL while the descriptor is still cached, but a crash or ESRCH would be equally conformant.
- Evidence: 2-1.c: `ret_val = pthread_join(new_th, NULL); if (ret_val != EINVAL) FAIL;` and the same for pthread_detach. POSIX pthread_join: "The behavior is undefined if the value specified by the thread argument to pthread_join() does not refer to a joinable thread." Change history: "The [EINVAL] error for a non-joinable thread is removed; this condition results in undefined behavior."
- Suggested action: Drop it, or replace it with a check that the detached thread's resources are released (e.g. create many detached threads and check that none fail with EAGAIN).
- Verification (phase 3, glibc vs musl build and libc sources): **CONFIRMED** via MUSL,RUN,SRC. HPE glibc: PASS (EINVAL: nptl/pthread_join_common.c:57-58, pthread_detach.c:42-43); musl: rc=139 SIGSEGV. musl pthread_join.c:17 a_crash() (hlt, arch/x86_64/atomic_arch.h:106-108) on a DT_DETACHED thread; if the thread already exited its map is gone. Conforming libc crashes on this UB.

- Category: UNDEF

### testcases/open_posix_testsuite/conformance/interfaces/pthread_barrier_wait/3-2.c  (openposix: conformance/interfaces/pthread_barrier_wait/3-2)
- Category: UNDEF  (secondary: FRAGILE)
- Confidence: high
- Claim under test: a thread interrupted by a signal while blocked on a barrier continues
  normally from the completed wait after its handler returns.
- Problem: the child's SIGUSR1 handler loops until `barrier_waited == 1`. Main sets that
  flag only after its own pthread_barrier_wait() returns. POSIX explicitly leaves
  unspecified whether other threads may proceed past the barrier while a participant is
  still inside a signal handler. An implementation that holds main until the handler
  returns therefore deadlocks, and the test hangs and times out, although it is conforming.
  glibc lets the last arriver return, so it passes there. Synchronization is
  sleep() polling on plain ints written from a signal handler and another thread
  (`sig_rcvd`, `barrier_waited` are not volatile/sig_atomic_t).
- Evidence: 3-2.c:41-52,126-141; the test's own header (3-2.c:10-12) and POSIX
  pthread_barrier_wait.html: "Until the thread in the signal handler returns from it, it is
  unspecified whether other threads may proceed past the barrier once they have all reached it."
- Suggested action: keep the handler short (set a volatile sig_atomic_t flag and return), and
  have main call barrier_wait only after the handler has returned. Alternatively, add an
  alarm/timeout that reports UNSUPPORTED rather than hanging when main blocks.
- Verification (phase 3, glibc vs musl build and libc sources): **UNCHANGED** via MUSL,RUN,REPEAT,SRC. HPE glibc: PASS 3/3 (main gets SERIAL); musl: PASS 3/3 (thread gets SERIAL). musl pthread_barrier_wait.c:93-110: last arriver returns without waiting for the instance owner, so musl, like glibc, does not hold main while the handler runs; the deadlocking implementation stays hypothetical. Finding rests on POSIX text; unchanged.

### testcases/open_posix_testsuite/conformance/interfaces/pthread_cancel/5-1.c  (openposix: conformance/interfaces/pthread_cancel/5-1)
- Category: UNDEF  (secondary: DOCS)
- Confidence: high
- Claim under test: pthread_cancel() "may" return ESRCH for a nonexistent thread.
- Problem: the test calls pthread_cancel() on a thread ID after pthread_join() has ended
  that thread's lifetime. Since Issue 7 (Austin Group interpretation #142), POSIX has no
  ESRCH for pthread_cancel(), and using a thread ID after its lifetime is undefined
  behaviour. With glibc the descriptor may already be freed or reused, so the call can
  touch freed memory, or cancel an unrelated, newly created thread that reuses the ID.
  The test accepts 0 and ESRCH, so in practice it only "fails" on another errno or a
  crash, and it exercises UB. The header still documents the removed ESRCH error.
- Evidence: 5-1.c:9-18,44-63; POSIX pthread_cancel.html ERRORS: only "shall not return an
  error code of [EINTR]"; CHANGE HISTORY Issue 7: "Austin Group Interpretation
  1003.1-2001 #142 is applied, removing the [ESRCH] error condition"; RATIONALE: "If an
  implementation detects use of a thread ID after the end of its lifetime, it is
  recommended that the function should fail and report an [ESRCH] error."
- Suggested action: drop the test.
- Verification (phase 3, glibc vs musl build and libc sources): **CONFIRMED** via MUSL,RUN,SRC. HPE glibc: PASS 'Returned 0' (nptl/pthread_cancel.c:62-68 returns 0 when joinstate==EXITED, TCB in stack cache); musl: rc=139 SIGSEGV: pthread_join.c:24 munmaps the thread map, then pthread_cancel.c:99 a_store(&t->cancel,1) writes to it. The predicted use-after-lifetime UAF happens on musl.

### testcases/open_posix_testsuite/conformance/interfaces/pthread_cond_init/4-3.c  (openposix: conformance/interfaces/pthread_cond_init/4-3)
- Category: UNDEF  (secondary: DOCS)
- Confidence: high (phase 1: medium)
- Claim under test: re-initializing an initialized condvar returns EBUSY (or 0).
- Problem: since Issue 7, POSIX has no EBUSY for pthread_cond_init(). Re-initializing an
  initialized condvar is undefined behaviour. The test demands 0 or EBUSY and FAILs on
  any other result, although any outcome is conforming. The header still describes EBUSY
  as the asserted behaviour.
- Evidence: 4-3.c:22-24,50-54; POSIX pthread_cond_destroy.html: "Attempting to initialize an
  already initialized condition variable results in undefined behavior." CHANGE HISTORY Issue 7:
  "The [EBUSY] error for a condition variable already in use or an already initialized
  condition variable is removed".
- Suggested action: drop the test, or report non-EBUSY results as UNSUPPORTED (as
  pthread_cond_destroy/speculative/4-1 does) instead of FAIL.
- Verification (phase 2, run on real hosts): **CONFIRMED** via RUN,READ. HPE: PASS (glibc returns 0 on re-init, so it cannot fail here). Code: second init must be 0 or EBUSY else PTS_FAIL. POSIX pthread_cond_destroy page (fetched): 'Attempting to initialize an already initialized condition variable results in undefined behavior'; Issue 7 removed EBUSY. Header still asserts EBUSY.
- Verification (phase 3, glibc vs musl build and libc sources): **CONFIRMED** via MUSL,RUN,SRC. HPE glibc: PASS; musl: PASS. Both re-init by zeroing (musl pthread_cond_init.c:5, glibc nptl/pthread_cond_init.c:32,49) and return 0; neither implements EBUSY, so the header's assertion is exercised by no tested libc and re-init of an in-use cond would strand waiters (UB).

### testcases/open_posix_testsuite/conformance/interfaces/pthread_cond_timedwait/1-1.c  (openposix: conformance/interfaces/pthread_cond_timedwait/1-1)
- Category: UNDEF
- Confidence: high (phase 1: medium)
- Claim under test: pthread_cond_timedwait() blocks on the condition variable.
- Problem: the waiter calls timedwait once, without a predicate loop. If it returns 0
  before main sets `signaled = 1`, the test prints "did not block on the cond at all" and
  returns PTS_FAIL. POSIX explicitly permits spurious wakeups, so a conforming
  implementation can fail this test. The sibling 2-1.c has the same code but returns
  PTS_UNRESOLVED for this case. On glibc with a single waiter this is rare in practice.
- Evidence: 1-1.c:56-74 (vs 2-1.c:197-200); POSIX pthread_cond_timedwait.html: "Spurious
  wakeups from the pthread_cond_clockwait(), pthread_cond_timedwait(), or
  pthread_cond_wait() functions may occur."
- Suggested action: loop on the predicate (re-wait while `signaled == 0` and rc == 0), or
  report UNRESOLVED like 2-1.c.
- Verification (phase 2, run on real hosts): **CONFIRMED** via RUN,MUTATION,REPEAT,STRESS,VIRT. As-is PASS (HPE 1, VIRT 3 + 3 under stress). Mutation simulating a spurious wakeup (extra pthread_cond_signal before main sets signaled=1) -> 'Thread1 did not block on the cond at all / Test FAILED' rc=1. POSIX (fetched): 'Spurious wakeups ... may occur'. Real glibc spurious wakeups are rare.
- Verification (phase 3, glibc vs musl build and libc sources): **UNCHANGED** via MUSL,RUN,REPEAT,SRC. HPE glibc: PASS 3/3; musl: PASS 3/3. musl pthread_cond_timedwait.c:100-102 re-waits while *fut==seq, so private condvars do not wake spuriously; :104-108 shows musl does return 'legitimate' spurious wakes for pshared condvars. Not observable here; phase-2 mutation stands.

### testcases/open_posix_testsuite/conformance/interfaces/pthread_cond_timedwait/2-2.c  (openposix: conformance/interfaces/pthread_cond_timedwait/2-2)
- Category: UNDEF
- Confidence: high (phase 1: medium)
- Claim under test: timedwait returns ETIMEDOUT when abstime passes before the cond is signalled.
- Problem: a single pthread_cond_timedwait() call must return ETIMEDOUT, and any other
  result, including 0, is PTS_FAIL. The cond is never signalled, so 0 can only be a
  spurious wakeup, which POSIX permits. Correct usage is to re-wait with the same abstime
  until ETIMEDOUT. Rare on glibc, but the test FAILs a conforming outcome.
- Evidence: 2-2.c:65-74; POSIX pthread_cond_timedwait.html: "Spurious wakeups ... may occur."
- Suggested action: `do rc = pthread_cond_timedwait(...); while (rc == 0);` and then
  require ETIMEDOUT.
- Verification (phase 2, run on real hosts): **CONFIRMED** via RUN,MUTATION,REPEAT,STRESS,VIRT. As-is PASS (HPE 1, VIRT 3 + 3 under stress). Mutation: one pthread_cond_signal while the thread waits (stand-in for a spurious wakeup) -> 'Test FAILED: pthread_cond_timedwait return 0 instead of ETIMEDOUT' rc=1. A single wait without re-wait loop FAILs a POSIX-permitted spurious return.
- Verification (phase 3, glibc vs musl build and libc sources): **UNCHANGED** via MUSL,RUN,REPEAT,SRC. HPE glibc: PASS 3/3; musl: PASS 3/3 'stops waiting when time is out'. musl pthread_cond_timedwait.c:100-102 returns ETIMEDOUT unless the futex word changed; spurious 0 needs a racing wake. Same as 1-1: both libcs suppress spurious wakeups; finding rests on POSIX text + phase-2 mutation.

### testcases/open_posix_testsuite/conformance/interfaces/pthread_detach/1-1.c  (openposix: conformance/interfaces/pthread_detach/1-1)
- Category: UNDEF
- Confidence: high
- Claim under test: after pthread_detach(), the thread is no longer joinable.
- Problem: Joins a detached thread and returns PASS only if pthread_join() returns EINVAL (0 is
  FAIL, anything else UNRESOLVED). POSIX.1-2024 makes this undefined behavior and lists no
  EINVAL error for pthread_join; EINVAL is only a RATIONALE recommendation. glibc happens to
  return EINVAL (IS_DETACHED check), so this passes on glibc but encodes UB.
- Evidence: 1-1.c `ret = pthread_join(new_th, NULL); ... else if (ret == EINVAL) PASS`;
  POSIX pthread_join: "The behavior is undefined if the value specified by the thread argument to
  pthread_join() does not refer to a joinable thread." ERRORS: only "may fail [EDEADLK]".
- Suggested action: accept any non-zero result, or drop. Detaching a joinable thread is better
  checked by showing that it still runs (2-2).
- Verification (phase 3, glibc vs musl build and libc sources): **CONFIRMED** via MUSL,RUN,SRC. HPE glibc: PASS (EINVAL, nptl/pthread_join_common.c:57-58); musl: rc=139 SIGSEGV: join of a detached thread hits pthread_join.c:17 a_crash() (deliberate trap) or the self-unmapped TCB. Test encodes glibc's EINVAL for UB.

### testcases/open_posix_testsuite/conformance/interfaces/pthread_detach/4-2.c  (openposix: conformance/interfaces/pthread_detach/4-2)
- Category: UNDEF
- Confidence: high
- Claim under test: pthread_detach() returns ESRCH for a non-existent thread.
- Problem: Joins the thread, then calls pthread_detach() on the same ID. After a join the thread
  ID's lifetime has ended (XBD 2.9.2), so any use is UB. On glibc the TCB has been handed to the
  stack cache (tid = -1), so ESRCH comes out by luck of the cache; if the stack were unmapped this
  would be a use-after-free. The test tolerates 0 (UNTESTED) but FAILs on any other code,
  e.g. EINVAL.
- Evidence: 4-2.c `pthread_join(new_th, NULL); ret = pthread_detach(new_th); if (ret != ESRCH)
  FAIL`; POSIX pthread_detach RATIONALE: "If an implementation detects use of a thread ID after
  the end of its lifetime, it is recommended that the function should fail and report an [ESRCH]
  error."
- Suggested action: drop.
- Verification (phase 3, glibc vs musl build and libc sources): **REVISED** via MUSL,RUN,SRC. HPE glibc: rc=5 UNTESTED 'does not return ESRCH' (returns 0: joinstate EXITED -> pthread_detach.c:37-46 -> clockjoin returns 0; nptl_free_tcb.c:27-28 guards the double free); musl: rc=139 SIGSEGV (pthread_join.c:24 unmapped the TCB, pthread_detach.c:8 a_cas on it). Phase-1 'glibc gives ESRCH by luck of cache' is wrong; never PASSes on either.
- Verification conclusion: The UB claim holds, but the glibc detail in the finding is wrong. glibc 2.43 does not return ESRCH "by luck of the cache". It returns 0: joinstate is still EXITED, so pthread_detach.c:37-46 calls __pthread_clockjoin_ex, which returns 0, and nptl_free_tcb.c:27-28 (TERMINATED_BITMASK) prevents a second free. The test therefore reports UNTESTED on glibc. On musl, the first join has unmapped the TCB (pthread_join.c:24) and pthread_detach.c:8 does a CAS on it, which crashes (SIGSEGV). Corrected finding: the test uses a thread ID after its lifetime has ended; it gives UNTESTED on glibc and crashes on musl, and can never PASS. Action: drop.

### testcases/open_posix_testsuite/conformance/interfaces/pthread_join/6-2.c  (openposix: conformance/interfaces/pthread_join/6-2)
- Category: UNDEF  (secondary: DOCS)
- Confidence: high
- Claim under test: "pthread_join() SHALL fail ... [ESRCH]" when it joins a thread that was already joined.
- Problem: In POSIX.1-2024, joining a thread that is no longer joinable, or whose ID lifetime has ended, is undefined behavior. The ESRCH error was removed (Interp. 1003.1-2001 #142). ESRCH and EINVAL survive only as RATIONALE recommendations. After commits 266dabb9df22 and faa34ecaddf5 the test returns UNTESTED on 0 (glibc 2.43 behavior), but it still returns FAIL for any other value, including EINVAL, which POSIX recommends for a non-joinable thread. The header text still cites ESRCH as "SHALL fail".
- Evidence: 6-2.c:10-12,66-75; https://pubs.opengroup.org/onlinepubs/9799919799/functions/pthread_join.html: "The behavior is undefined if the value specified by the thread argument to pthread_join() does not refer to a joinable thread." CHANGE HISTORY: "Austin Group Interpretation 1003.1-2001 #142 is applied, removing the [ESRCH] error condition."
- Suggested action: Drop the test, or report UNTESTED for every outcome other than ESRCH. Fix the header to describe ESRCH as a recommendation for UB.
- Verification (phase 3, glibc vs musl build and libc sources): **CONFIRMED** via MUSL,RUN,SRC. HPE glibc: rc=5 UNTESTED (second join returns 0: joinstate stays EXITED, nptl_free_tcb.c:27-28 guards free); musl: rc=139 SIGSEGV: first join munmapped the TCB (pthread_join.c:24), second join reads t->detach_state (:16). Joining an ended thread ID is UB with a crash on musl.

### testcases/open_posix_testsuite/conformance/interfaces/pthread_key_create/speculative/5-1.c  (openposix: conformance/interfaces/pthread_key_create/speculative/5-1)
- Category: UNDEF
- Confidence: high (phase 1: medium)
- Claim under test: creating more than PTHREAD_KEYS_MAX keys returns EAGAIN.
- Problem: The test returns FAIL ("EAGAIN returned before the key limit was exceeded") if EAGAIN comes before the test itself has created PTHREAD_KEYS_MAX keys. POSIX also allows EAGAIN when "the system lacked the necessary resources", and keys used internally by libc or other libraries in the process count toward the per-process limit. An early EAGAIN therefore conforms.
- Evidence: speculative/5-1.c:47-67; pthread_key_create(3p) ERRORS: "[EAGAIN] The system lacked the necessary resources to create another thread-specific data key, or the system-imposed limit on the total number of keys per process {PTHREAD_KEYS_MAX} has been exceeded."
- Suggested action: Accept EAGAIN at any i >= 1 (it is the documented outcome). Fail only when more than PTHREAD_KEYS_MAX keys succeed, or when a different error comes back.
- Verification (phase 2, run on real hosts): **CONFIRMED** via RUN,MUTATION. HPE: PASS as-is. LD_PRELOAD of a 3-line .so whose constructor calls pthread_key_create once (like any library using TSD) -> 'EAGAIN returned before the key limit was exceeded' rc=1 (FAIL). POSIX (fetched): EAGAIN when 'the total number of keys per process' exceeds PTHREAD_KEYS_MAX, so it is conforming.
- Verification (phase 3, glibc vs musl build and libc sources): **CONFIRMED** via MUSL,RUN,SRC. HPE glibc: PASS; musl: PASS. musl PTHREAD_KEYS_MAX=128 (limits.h:66), one process-wide table (pthread_key_create.c:7) also used by C11 tss_create (tss_create.c:9); glibc 1024 (local_lim.h:64). Neither libc uses keys internally, so PASS; any library key -> early EAGAIN -> FAIL (phase-2 LD_PRELOAD mutation).

### testcases/open_posix_testsuite/conformance/interfaces/pthread_mutex_init/1-2.c  (openposix: conformance/interfaces/pthread_mutex_init/1-2)
- Category: UNDEF
- Confidence: high (phase 1: low)
- Claim under test: a mutex initialized with NULL attr behaves the same as one initialized with a default attr object.
- Problem: The behaviors compared are unlocking an unlocked mutex, unlocking a mutex owned by another thread, and relocking an owned mutex. All three are undefined for PTHREAD_MUTEX_DEFAULT unless DEFAULT maps to one of the other types. The relock subcase also uses PTHREAD_CANCEL_ASYNCHRONOUS around pthread_mutex_lock(), which is not async-cancel-safe. glibc behaves the same for both mutexes, so there is no false FAIL in practice, but the test relies on UB, and on glibc the first step leaves __nusers wrapped.
- Evidence: 1-2.c:216-217,249,124; pthread_mutex_lock.html: for DEFAULT, "the behavior is undefined for the cases marked" (relock, unlock when not owner).
- Suggested action: Compare observable defined properties (gettype/getprotocol/getpshared through the attr, trylock EBUSY by another thread), or document that the test relies on DEFAULT mapping to a defined type.
- Verification (phase 2, run on real hosts): **CONFIRMED** via RUN,READ. HPE: rc=0, 'Results for deadlock issue: mutex 1/2 deadlock did not return 0'. Compares unlock-unlocked, unlock-by-non-owner and relock on two DEFAULT mutexes; POSIX pthread_mutex_lock table (fetched) marks these 'undefined behavior' for DEFAULT unless it maps to NORMAL/ERRORCHECK/RECURSIVE. glibc equal for both -> no false FAIL.
- Verification (phase 3, glibc vs musl build and libc sources): **CONFIRMED** via MUSL,RUN,SRC. HPE glibc: PASS ('deadlock did not return 0'); musl: HANG, killed at 120 s rc=124; child in futex_do_wait (relock), main in join. musl __timedwait.c:63-70 disables cancel around the futex wait (from pthread_mutex_timedlock.c:85), so async SIGCANCEL is ignored (pthread_cancel.c:55). mutex_lock is not async-cancel-safe: musl conforms.

### testcases/open_posix_testsuite/conformance/interfaces/pthread_mutex_timedlock/5-1.c  (openposix: conformance/interfaces/pthread_mutex_timedlock/5-1)
- Category: UNDEF
- Confidence: high (phase 1: medium)
- Claim under test: EINVAL when the call would block and abs_timeout.tv_nsec < 0.
- Problem: "Would have blocked" is set up by having the thread relock a DEFAULT-type mutex that it already owns (f1 locks &mutex and then timedlocks it). POSIX makes relocking a DEFAULT mutex undefined unless the type behaves like NORMAL/ERRORCHECK/RECURSIVE. pthread_mutex_timedlock also "may fail [EDEADLK] A deadlock condition was detected", so a conforming implementation can return EDEADLK (or 0 for recursive-like behavior), and the test then returns FAIL. It passes on glibc only because glibc validates tv_nsec before the deadlock.
- Evidence: 5-1.c:86-98; pthread_mutex_timedlock.html: "may fail if: [EDEADLK] A deadlock condition was detected."; pthread_mutex_lock.html table: relock of DEFAULT is undefined (marked with a dagger).
- Suggested action: Have main (or another thread) hold the mutex, as 5-3.c does, and call timedlock from a non-owner thread.
- Verification (phase 2, run on real hosts): **CONFIRMED** via RUN,MUTATION,READ. HPE: PASS as-is (glibc NORMAL checks tv_nsec first). Mutated only the mutex init to PTHREAD_ERRORCHECK_MUTEX_INITIALIZER_NP (a mapping POSIX allows for DEFAULT, per the mutex_lock table dagger) -> 'Test FAILED: Expected return code EINVAL, got: 35' (EDEADLK). EDEADLK is a POSIX may-fail for timedlock.
- Verification (phase 3, glibc vs musl build and libc sources): **CONFIRMED** via MUSL,RUN,SRC. HPE glibc: PASS; musl: PASS. Both default to NORMAL and both check EDEADLK for ERRORCHECK before tv_nsec: musl pthread_mutex_timedlock.c:78-80 vs __timedwait.c:41; glibc nptl/pthread_mutex_timedlock.c:78 vs :208-209. PASS depends on DEFAULT==NORMAL in both libcs; EDEADLK mapping (phase-2 mutation) FAILs.

### testcases/open_posix_testsuite/conformance/interfaces/pthread_mutexattr_destroy/4-1.c  (openposix: conformance/interfaces/pthread_mutexattr_destroy/4-1)
- Category: UNDEF  (secondary: WEAK)
- Confidence: high (phase 1: medium)
- Claim under test: [EINVAL] for an invalid attr.
- Problem: The test passes a NULL pointer, which is UB (the EINVAL error is no longer required; it is only recommended for a detected invalid object). Both branches return PTS_PASS, so the test can never fail on a libc that returns any value. It can only "fail" by crashing on a libc that dereferences attr. glibc's pthread_mutexattr_destroy() ignores its argument and returns 0.

Both branches return PTS_PASS, so only a crash could fail it. POSIX (fetched): destroy on a non-initialized attr is UB; EINVAL only recommended in RATIONALE, removed in Issue 7.
- Verification (phase 3, glibc vs musl build and libc sources): **CONFIRMED** via MUSL,RUN,SRC. HPE glibc: PASS 'Expect 22(EINVAL), but return 0'; musl: same. Both ignore attr: musl pthread_mutexattr_destroy.c:3-6, glibc nptl/pthread_mutexattr_destroy.c:23-26. Test can only fail by crashing.

- Verification (phase 2, run on real hosts): **CONFIRMED** via RUN,READ. HPE: rc=5 'UNTESTED: The call didn't fail.' (glibc returns 0 on a zeroed attr). Any result other than 0/EINVAL is FAIL. POSIX gettype page (fetched): uninitialized attr is UB; Issue 7: 'The [EINVAL] error for an uninitialized mutex attributes object is removed'.
- Verification (phase 3, glibc vs musl build and libc sources): **CONFIRMED** via MUSL,RUN,SRC. HPE glibc and musl (pthread_mutexattr_gettype_speculative_3-1.run-test): rc=5 'UNTESTED: The call didn't fail.' Both return 0 unconditionally: musl src/thread/pthread_attr_get.c:88-92, glibc nptl/pthread_mutexattr_gettype.c:28-30 -> EINVAL path unreachable, UNTESTED on every Linux libc

### testcases/open_posix_testsuite/conformance/interfaces/pthread_mutexattr_setprioceiling/3-2.c  (openposix: conformance/interfaces/pthread_mutexattr_setprioceiling/3-2)
- Category: UNDEF (phase 1: WRONG)  (secondary: UNDEF, WEAK)

Both reject the value before touching attr: musl src/thread/pthread_mutexattr_setpshared.c:5 'if (pshared > 1U) return EINVAL', glibc nptl/pthread_mutexattr_setpshared.c:27-28 -> result reflects the out-of-range value on both libcs; missing init is latent UB

### testcases/open_posix_testsuite/conformance/interfaces/pthread_once/3-1.c  (openposix: conformance/interfaces/pthread_once/3-1)
- Category: UNDEF
- Confidence: medium
- Claim under test: if init_routine is cancelled at a cancellation point, once_control behaves as if pthread_once() was never called.
- Problem: The thread sets PTHREAD_CANCEL_ASYNCHRONOUS and then calls pthread_once(), sleep() and perror(), none of which are async-cancel-safe; POSIX makes that undefined (only pthread_cancel/setcancelstate/setcanceltype are async-cancel-safe). The assertion is about init_routine being a cancellation point, which deferred cancellation of sleep() already exercises. Additionally init_flag is a plain int polled across threads (data race), and init functions of type `void *(*)()` are cast to `void (*)(void)` and called through it (UB in C).
- Evidence: 3-1.c:35, 55-57, 81-82, 104; POSIX XSH 2.9.5.4 "Async-Cancel Safety": only pthread_cancel(), pthread_setcancelstate(), pthread_setcanceltype() are async-cancel-safe; pthread_once DESCRIPTION: "if init_routine is a cancellation point and is canceled, the effect on once_control shall be as if pthread_once() was never called."
- Suggested action: drop the setcanceltype(ASYNCHRONOUS) call (use default deferred cancel), fix the init function prototypes to `void f(void)`, use a semaphore/volatile flag for the handshake.
- Verification (phase 2, run on real hosts): **CONFIRMED** via RUN,MUTATION,REPEAT,STRESS,VIRT. HPE 1x + 3x stress, VIRT 5x: all Test PASSED (glibc copes with async cancel inside sleep()). Mutant without pthread_setcanceltype(ASYNCHRONOUS) (deferred cancel, sleep() is a cancellation point): Test PASSED -> async type is unnecessary. UB only by POSIX text (man pthread_setcancelstate(3): only cancel/setcancelstate/setcanceltype are async-cancel-safe); cannot be shown by running
- Verification (phase 3, glibc vs musl build and libc sources): **UNCHANGED** via MUSL,RUN,REPEAT,SRC. HPE glibc PASS; musl PASS 6/6 (1 + ltprepeat 5). Async cancel inside sleep() works on both: musl src/thread/pthread_cancel.c:59-62 (cancel_handler calls __cancel when cancelasync), glibc nptl/pthread_cancel.c:50-54; musl undo() (pthread_once.c:3-9) resets control. UB remains by POSIX text only

### testcases/open_posix_testsuite/conformance/interfaces/pthread_once/6-1.c  (openposix: conformance/interfaces/pthread_once/6-1)

### testcases/open_posix_testsuite/conformance/interfaces/pthread_rwlock_timedrdlock/6-2.c  (openposix: conformance/interfaces/pthread_rwlock_timedrdlock/6-2)
- Category: UNDEF  (secondary: FRAGILE)
- Confidence: medium
- Claim under test: after a signal handler returns, a thread blocked in timedrdlock resumes waiting "as if it was not interrupted", and gets the lock without ETIMEDOUT.
- Problem: Timeline: deadline = t0+2s; signal at ~t0+1; the handler sleeps 4s (until ~t0+5); main unlocks at ~t0+3, i.e. after the deadline. Had the thread not been interrupted, it would have timed out at t0+2, so "as if it was not interrupted" supports ETIMEDOUT. The test nevertheless FAILs on ETIMEDOUT and requires rc==0. POSIX does not order these: the "shall not fail with a timeout if the lock can be acquired immediately" sentence is about the call itself, not about resuming. glibc happens to re-check the lock first. Also, the main thread's "wait for handler to be sleeping" handshake is dead code: th_fn() sets handler_state = 2 before blocking, so `while (handler_state != 2 ...)` exits after the first sleep(2) and the `handler_state == 1` check can never trigger. Synchronization is purely sleep-based.
- Evidence: 6-2.c:47 (TIMEOUT 2), 62-72 (handler sleeps 4s), 86 (handler_state = 2), 166-177, 184-206; https://pubs.opengroup.org/onlinepubs/9799919799/functions/pthread_rwlock_timedrdlock.html: "upon return from the signal handler the thread shall resume waiting for the lock as if it was not interrupted."
- Suggested action: accept both 0 and ETIMEDOUT (just check the call returns and does not report EINTR), or unlock before the deadline; initialise handler_state to 1 so the handshake works.
- Verification (phase 2, run on real hosts): **CONFIRMED** via RUN,MUTATION,REPEAT,STRESS,VIRT. HPE: PASS in 5.05 s ('main: unlock write lock' at ~t0+3 after the t0+2 deadline, lock taken at ~t0+5); HPE 2x+3x stress, VIRT 2x stress all PASS (glibc rechecks the lock first). Mutant without pthread_kill(): 'Error: thread timeout in sig_handler' rc=2, never 'signal handler did not get called' -> handler_state handshake is dead (th_fn presets 2)
- Verification (phase 3, glibc vs musl build and libc sources): **UNCHANGED** via MUSL,RUN,REPEAT,SRC. HPE glibc PASS; musl PASS 6/6, ~5 s. musl src/thread/pthread_rwlock_timedrdlock.c:13-21 treats EINTR as 'retry' and calls tryrdlock before re-waiting (lock free since t0+3); __timedwait_cp (__timedwait.c:41-48) would report ETIMEDOUT only on the next wait. Same order as glibc; ETIMEDOUT stays a conforming outcome by POSIX text

### testcases/open_posix_testsuite/conformance/interfaces/pthread_rwlock_timedwrlock/6-2.c  (openposix: conformance/interfaces/pthread_rwlock_timedwrlock/6-2)

"As if it was not interrupted" would then give ETIMEDOUT, but the test FAILs on ETIMEDOUT. The handler_state handshake is dead: th_fn() pre-sets handler_state = 2.
- Evidence: 6-2.c (TIMEOUT 2, handler sleep(TIMEOUT*2), th_fn `handler_state = 2;`, main `if (expired == 1) FAIL`); POSIX pthread_rwlock_timedwrlock: "upon return from the signal handler the thread shall resume waiting for the lock as if it was not interrupted."
- Suggested action: accept 0 or ETIMEDOUT, or release the lock before the deadline; fix handler_state init.

Mutant without pthread_kill(): 'thread: timer expired' + 'Error: thread timeout in sig_handler' rc=2, the 'signal handler did not get called' check never fires -> same dead handshake as timedrdlock/6-2

### testcases/open_posix_testsuite/conformance/interfaces/pthread_rwlock_trywrlock/speculative/3-1.c  (openposix: conformance/interfaces/pthread_rwlock_trywrlock/speculative/3-1)
- Category: UNDEF  (secondary: WRONG)
- Confidence: high (phase 1: medium)
- Claim under test: trywrlock may fail with EINVAL on an uninitialized rwlock.
- Problem: Using an uninitialized rwlock has been undefined since POSIX.1-2008 (the EINVAL error was removed). The logic is also self-defeating: it calls pthread_rwlock_unlock() and pthread_rwlock_destroy() on the same object *before* checking rc, so an implementation that does detect the uninitialized lock (returns EINVAL) would also fail the unlock and exit UNRESOLVED. The PASS-on-EINVAL branch is effectively unreachable. On glibc a zeroed static rwlock equals PTHREAD_RWLOCK_INITIALIZER, so rc is 0 and the test just passes.
- Evidence: speculative/3-1.c:26-55; https://pubs.opengroup.org/onlinepubs/9799919799/functions/pthread_rwlock_trywrlock.html (CHANGE HISTORY Issue 7: EINVAL for uninitialized rwlock removed, behaviour undefined).
- Suggested action: drop.
- Verification (phase 2, run on real hosts): **CONFIRMED** via RUN,READ. HPE: 'Test PASSED: Note*: Returned 0 instead of EINVAL' rc=0 (zeroed static rwlock == initializer on glibc). POSIX 2024: 'Results are undefined if any of these functions are called with an uninitialized read-write lock'; Issue 7: '[EINVAL] error for an uninitialized read-write lock object is removed'. unlock/destroy run before rc is examined (3-1.c:33-41). Drop
- Verification (phase 3, glibc vs musl build and libc sources): **CONFIRMED** via MUSL,RUN,SRC. HPE glibc and musl (pthread_rwlock_trywrlock_speculative_3-1.run-test): rc=0 'Returned 0 instead of EINVAL'. musl src/thread/pthread_rwlock_trywrlock.c:5 just CASes 0->0x7fffffff (zeroed static == initializer); no validity check in either libc -> EINVAL branch unreachable

### testcases/open_posix_testsuite/conformance/interfaces/pthread_rwlock_wrlock/3-1.c  (openposix: conformance/interfaces/pthread_rwlock_wrlock/3-1)
- Category: UNDEF
- Confidence: high (phase 1: medium)
- Claim under test: wrlock may fail with EDEADLK when the caller already holds the write lock.
- Problem: POSIX.1-2024 says that in this case "the call shall either deadlock or return [EDEADLK]". Deadlock is therefore a conforming outcome, and the test hangs until the harness timeout and is counted as a failure. musl does not track rwlock owners and deadlocks here. Conversely the test accepts rc==0 (double write-acquire), which POSIX does not allow. glibc returns EDEADLK, so it passes there.
- Evidence: 3-1.c:46-79; https://pubs.opengroup.org/onlinepubs/9799919799/functions/pthread_rwlock_trywrlock.html (pthread_rwlock_wrlock): "...the calling thread already owns the read-write lock for writing or reading, the call shall either deadlock or return [EDEADLK]."
- Suggested action: use alarm()/timed variant to treat a deadlock as PASS/UNTESTED, and stop accepting 0.
- Verification (phase 2, run on real hosts): **CONFIRMED** via RUN,MUTATION,READ. HPE: 'main: correctly got EDEADLK / Test PASSED'. VIRT mutant where the 2nd wrlock 'succeeds' (rc = 0, double write acquire): 'Test PASSED: Note*: Returned 0 instead of EDEADLK' rc=0 -> a non-conforming result passes. POSIX 2024 re-checked: '...already owns the read-write lock for writing or reading, the call shall either deadlock or return [EDEADLK]' -> deadlock (musl) would time out
- Verification (phase 3, glibc vs musl build and libc sources): **CONFIRMED** via MUSL,RUN,SRC. HPE glibc: 'main: correctly got EDEADLK / Test PASSED' (nptl/pthread_rwlock_common.c:596-599 checks __cur_writer). musl: hangs after 'main: attempt write lock', killed rc=124 at LTPRUN_TIMEOUT=40: no owner tracking (src/thread/pthread_rwlock_timedwrlock.c:13-21 just waits) -> conforming deadlock reported as hang/failure

### testcases/open_posix_testsuite/conformance/interfaces/pthread_setcancelstate/1-1.c  (openposix: conformance/interfaces/pthread_setcancelstate/1-1)
- Category: UNDEF

In general, other library functions can't be safely called from an asynchronously cancelable thread." and "POSIX.1 does not specify this point [NULL oldstate]".

- Verification (phase 3, glibc vs musl build and libc sources): **UNCHANGED** via MUSL,RUN,REPEAT,SRC. HPE glibc PASS; musl PASS 6/6. Async cancel during sleep() works on both: musl src/thread/pthread_cancel.c:59-62 calls __cancel from cancel_handler when cancelasync, glibc nptl/pthread_cancel.c:50-54. UB by POSIX text only; contrast pthread_setcanceltype/1-1 where musl differs

### testcases/open_posix_testsuite/conformance/interfaces/pthread_setcanceltype/1-1.c  (openposix: conformance/interfaces/pthread_setcanceltype/1-1)
- Category: UNDEF
- Confidence: high (phase 1: medium)
- Claim under test: with PTHREAD_CANCEL_ASYNCHRONOUS a cancel request is acted on immediately.
- Problem: The thread enables async cancellation and then blocks in pthread_mutex_lock(), which is not async-cancel-safe. POSIX leaves async cancellation inside such a call undefined, and it can leave the mutex internals inconsistent. The test requires the cleanup handler to run within 10s. A well-defined async-cancel test needs a pure compute loop (no library calls) in the target thread.
- Evidence: 1-1.c:53-67, 104-124; man pthread_setcancelstate(3) NOTES: "other library functions can't be safely called from an asynchronously cancelable thread"; "One of the few circumstances in which asynchronous cancelability is useful is for cancelation of a thread that is in a pure compute-bound loop."
- Suggested action: replace the mutex wait with a busy loop on a volatile flag (no library calls) after enabling async cancel.
- Verification (phase 2, run on real hosts): **CONFIRMED** via RUN,REPEAT,STRESS,VIRT,READ. HPE 1x + 3x stress, VIRT 5x: all Test PASSED (cleanup handler ran). Not mutable without changing the test's subject; man pthread_setcancelstate(3) NOTES: 'other library functions can't be safely called from an asynchronously cancelable thread' - here the target is blocked in pthread_mutex_lock(), so the result relies on glibc behaviour
- Verification (phase 3, glibc vs musl build and libc sources): **CONFIRMED** via MUSL,RUN,REPEAT,SRC. HPE glibc PASS 4/4; musl FAIL 6/6 'Test FAILED: Cancel request timed out'. musl mutex lock waits in __timedwait(), which disables cancellation around the futex wait (src/thread/__timedwait.c:67-69, pthread_mutex_timedlock.c:85), so cancel_handler returns early (pthread_cancel.c:55); glibc sigcancel_handler (nptl/pthread_cancel.c:50-54) exits anyway

### testcases/open_posix_testsuite/conformance/interfaces/sigaction/10-1.c  (openposix: conformance/interfaces/sigaction/10-1)
- Category: UNDEF  (secondary: FRAGILE)
- Confidence: high
- Claim under test: assertion #10, SIGCHLD is generated when a child stops (SA_NOCLDSTOP clear).
- Problem: PASS requires `child_stopped == NUMSTOPS && child_continued == NUMSTOPS`, i.e. it also
  demands a CLD_CONTINUED SIGCHLD for every SIGCONT. POSIX only says SIGCHLD "may" be generated when a
  stopped child is continued (that is assertion #11, XSI). Linux does send it, so this passes on Linux,
  but the check is stronger than the assertion. Also: waits use 1 s select() timeouts (a late SIGCHLD
  can coalesce with the next one since SIGCHLD does not queue), printf() in the handler, and failure is
  `return -1` (exit 255) instead of PTS_FAIL.
- Evidence: 10-1.c:113; https://pubs.opengroup.org/onlinepubs/9799919799/functions/sigaction.html
  SA_NOCLDSTOP: SIGCHLD "shall be generated ... whenever any of its child processes stop" and "may be
  generated ... whenever any of its stopped child processes are continued".
- Suggested action: Check only child_stopped == NUMSTOPS (leave CLD_CONTINUED to 11-1); return PTS_FAIL.

### testcases/open_posix_testsuite/conformance/interfaces/sigaddset/2-1.c  (runtest: openposix: conformance/interfaces/sigaddset/2-1)
- Category: UNDEF  (secondary: DOCS)
- Confidence: high
- Claim under test: sigaddset() on a sigset_t that was never initialized must not crash or hang.
  The header says the test passes whenever the system is able to report a result.
- Problem: The code returns PTS_FAIL unless sigaddset() returns 0 and sigismember() then returns 1.
  That demands a specific outcome for behavior POSIX declares undefined, and the test reads an
  indeterminate automatic object. glibc and musl just OR in the bit, so it passes in practice, but
  the assertion contradicts both the spec and the test's own description.
- Evidence: testcases/open_posix_testsuite/conformance/interfaces/sigaddset/2-1.c:21-33; POSIX.1-2024 sigaddset DESCRIPTION: "If such an object is not
  initialized in this way, but is nonetheless supplied as an argument to any of ... sigaddset() ...
  the results are undefined."; sigsetops(3): "The results are undefined if this is not done."
- Suggested action: Return PTS_PASS for any return value (as the header says), or drop the test.
- Verification (phase 3, glibc vs musl build and libc sources): **CONFIRMED** via MUSL,RUN,SRC. HPE glibc: 'Test PASSED: Signal was added' rc 0; musl: same rc 0. Both just OR in the bit without reading the rest of the set: glibc signal/sigaddset.c:27-34, musl src/signal/sigaddset.c:6-12. Claim about both libcs verified; test still demands an outcome for UB, contradicting its header

### testcases/open_posix_testsuite/conformance/interfaces/sigaddset/4-1.c  (runtest: openposix: conformance/interfaces/sigaddset/4-1)
- Category: UNDEF

  returns -1/EINVAL.
- Problem: POSIX lists EINVAL for sigaddset() only under "may fail", so a conforming
  implementation can accept or ignore an invalid signo. The test FAILs unless EINVAL is
  returned. On Linux this does not cause false failures: sigsetops(3) lists EINVAL
  unconditionally, and both glibc and musl range-check signo. As a POSIX conformance test it is
  still too strict.

- Suggested action: Accept ret==0 as PASS (or return PTS_UNSUPPORTED). Keep requiring errno==EINVAL
  when -1 is returned.
- Verification (phase 2, run on real hosts): **CONFIRMED** via RUN,READ,GIT. HPE: sigaddset_4-1 Test PASSED as-is (glibc 2.43 returns -1/EINVAL for all 4 values). opengroup.org Issue 8 sigaddset ERRORS re-fetched: 'The sigaddset() function may fail if: [EINVAL]' -> requiring EINVAL is stricter than POSIX; no Linux false-fail (sigsetops(3) lists EINVAL). Test written 2013 (e23ac119aa0b) from XSH6 assertion 5 wording 'will return'.
- Verification (phase 3, glibc vs musl build and libc sources): **CONFIRMED** via MUSL,RUN,SRC. HPE glibc: Test PASSED rc 0; musl: Test PASSED rc 0. Both range-check: glibc signal/sigaddset.c:27-31 (signo<=0||>=NSIG||internal), musl src/signal/sigaddset.c:7 (sig-1>=_NSIG-1 || 32..34) -> no Linux false fail; POSIX still 'may fail' EINVAL, so too strict as conformance test

### testcases/open_posix_testsuite/conformance/interfaces/sigprocmask/15-1.c  (openposix: conformance/interfaces/sigprocmask/15-1)
- Category: UNDEF  (secondary: DOCS, WEAK)

POSIX says results are undefined for an uninitialised sigset_t, so the test blocks an arbitrary stack-garbage set of signals. On Linux this cannot make the call fail (the kernel silently drops SIGKILL/SIGSTOP and ignores bits above _NSIG), so the test only checks "returns 0". The header is copied from sigignore/4-1.
- Evidence: sigprocmask/15-1.c:3,14-17; POSIX sigismember/sigaddset: "Applications should call either sigemptyset() or sigfillset() at least once for each object of type sigset_t prior to any other use of that object. If such an object is not initialized in this way ... the results are undefined."
- Suggested action: add sigemptyset(&set) and fix the header.
- Verification (phase 2, run on real hosts): **CONFIRMED** via RUN,MUTATION,READ,GIT. HPE: as-is PASS. Mutant memset(&set,0xff) before sigaddset (models worst-case stack garbage) still 'Test PASSED' with SigBlk fffffffe7ffbfeff (all but SIGKILL/SIGSTOP and glibc-internal 32/33) -> uninitialised set is used, call cannot fail on Linux, only 'returns 0' is checked. Header line 8 says 'if sigignore returns a 0'.
- Verification (phase 3, glibc vs musl build and libc sources): **CONFIRMED** via MUSL,RUN,SRC. HPE glibc: Test PASSED rc 0; musl: Test PASSED rc 0. musl src/thread/pthread_sigmask.c:8-9 passes the (uninitialised) set straight to rt_sigprocmask with no validation, kernel drops SIGKILL/STOP -> call cannot fail under either libc; only 'returns 0' checked

### testcases/open_posix_testsuite/conformance/interfaces/sigwaitinfo/6-1.c  (openposix: conformance/interfaces/sigwaitinfo/6-1)
- Category: UNDEF  (secondary: DOCS)
- Confidence: high
- Claim under test: info->si_code records the cause of the signal; the test requires SI_USER for a signal generated by raise(). The header text is copied from 5-1 and talks about si_signo.
- Problem: POSIX only requires SI_USER for kill(): "SI_USER: Signal sent by kill()". For raise() it says "The implementation may set si_code to SI_USER if the signal was sent by the raise() or abort() functions...", which makes SI_USER optional. On Linux, a thread-directed signal (tgkill/tkill) gets si_code = SI_TKILL (kernel/signal.c:4009 prepare_kill_siginfo, used by do_tkill at 4227). glibc's raise() currently yields SI_USER (verified: si_code=0 on this host), but musl's raise() uses tkill and yields SI_TKILL (-6), so the test FAILs on a conforming system.
- Evidence: sigwaitinfo/6-1.c:3-4,48,55-58; https://pubs.opengroup.org/onlinepubs/9799919799/functions/V2_chap02.html 2.4.3 SI_USER; /usr/src/linux/kernel/signal.c:4009,4227.
- Suggested action: generate the signal with kill(getpid(), SIGTOTEST) (which must give SI_USER), or accept SI_USER and SI_TKILL; fix the header.
- Verification (phase 3, glibc vs musl build and libc sources): **REVISED** via MUSL,RUN,SRC. HPE glibc: PASS; musl: FAIL rc=1 'The cause of the signal hasn't been stored in the si_code'. Probe: raise->sigwaitinfo si_code glibc 0, musl -6; SA_SIGINFO handler -6 on both. glibc raise also uses tgkill (nptl/pthread_kill.c:43) but sigtimedwait.c:57-62 folds SI_TKILL->SI_USER; musl raise.c:10 tkill, sigtimedwait.c no fold
- Verification conclusion: The test fails on musl for exactly the stated reason. The finding is right. But "glibc's raise() yields SI_USER" is wrong. glibc raise() (sysdeps/posix/raise.c:26 -> nptl/pthread_kill.c:42-43) uses tgkill, so the kernel sets SI_TKILL (kernel/signal.c:4009,4227). glibc's sigtimedwait wrapper then rewrites SI_TKILL to SI_USER (sysdeps/unix/sysv/linux/sigtimedwait.c:57-62). musl raise.c:10 uses tkill and its sigtimedwait.c does no such rewrite. A SA_SIGINFO handler sees -6 on both libcs. Corrected text: "glibc passes only because its sigwaitinfo/sigtimedwait wrapper folds SI_TKILL into SI_USER." The action stays the same: use kill(getpid(), SIGTOTEST), or accept SI_TKILL. Fix the header.

### testcases/open_posix_testsuite/conformance/interfaces/strncpy/1-1.c  (openposix: conformance/interfaces/strncpy/1-1)
- Category: UNDEF  (secondary: WEAK)
- Confidence: high
- Claim under test: strncpy() copies at most n bytes and returns s2.
- Problem: the destination is `malloc(i - 1)`, and n = rand() % i can be as large as i - 1. strncpy() itself can write i-1 bytes (in bounds), but the following `sample_str_2[num_bytes] = '\0'` writes index i-1, one byte past the allocation. For i == 1 it is malloc(0) and writes byte 0. This heap out-of-bounds write is UB; it usually lands in malloc padding, so it passes by luck, and it fails under ASan/hardened allocators. The "bytes that follow a NUL character are not copied" part of the assertion is never exercised, because the source has no NUL before n.
- Evidence: strncpy/1-1.c:53,59,61,63.
- Suggested action: allocate i + 1 bytes (or num_bytes + 1). Add a source with an embedded NUL before n and check that the destination beyond it is NUL-padded.

### testcases/open_posix_testsuite/conformance/interfaces/strncpy/2-1.c  (openposix: conformance/interfaces/strncpy/2-1)
- Category: UNDEF
- Confidence: high
- Claim under test: when the source is shorter than n, strncpy() pads with NUL up to n bytes.
- Problem: the destination is `malloc(i + EXTRA_BYTES)` and strncpy() writes exactly i + EXTRA_BYTES bytes. The following `sample_str_2[i + EXTRA_BYTES] = '\0'` then writes one byte past the allocation, which is UB. That line is also pointless, since strncpy already NUL-padded. A content mismatch is reported as PTS_UNRESOLVED instead of FAIL.
- Evidence: strncpy/2-1.c:54,60-67.
- Suggested action: remove line 61 (or allocate one more byte), and return PTS_FAIL on a mismatch.

### testcases/open_posix_testsuite/conformance/interfaces/timer_delete/1-2.c  (openposix: conformance/interfaces/timer_delete/1-2)
- Category: UNDEF
- Confidence: medium
- Claim under test: after timer_delete(), timer_settime() on that id fails with EINVAL.
- Problem: POSIX.1-2024 timer_settime(): "The behavior is undefined if the value specified by the timerid argument ... does not correspond to a timer ID returned by timer_create() but not yet deleted by timer_delete()". The EINVAL was made optional in Issue 6 and is only "recommended" in RATIONALE. Sibling speculative/5-1 was relaxed in d377d1cff1ec/ba58ac3254d6; 1-2 was not.

## FRAGILE: Racy, timing-dependent or environment-dependent

The test can report FAIL on a correct system because of sleep-based synchronization, scheduler or CPU assumptions, filesystem or kernel-config assumptions without detection, hardware or distro defaults. Action: add proper synchronization or detection (TCONF), or drop.

190 testcases. Sorted by path; confidence shown in each entry.

### testcases/commands/unshare/unshare01.sh  (runtest: commands/unshare01_sh)
- Category: FRAGILE
- Confidence: high (phase 1: medium)
- Claim under test: test 6, `unshare --mount --propagation shared mount --bind dir_A dir_B`, makes the bind mount visible in the parent mount namespace.
- Problem: Propagation back to the parent only happens if the mount that holds the LTP tmpdir is already shared in the parent namespace. When a mount namespace is copied, the new mount joins the peer group of the old one only if the old one has a group id; a private parent mount gives a private copy, and unshare's `--propagation shared` then creates a new peer group that does not include the parent. Systemd makes / shared by default, so the test passes there, but it fails on correct kernels under non-systemd init, in containers, or with TMPDIR on a private mount. Tests 1/2 also hard-code 65534, which is /proc/sys/kernel/overflowuid and overflowgid (tunable, user_namespaces(7)), not a fixed value.
- Evidence: unshare01.sh:150-151; fs/namespace.c:1338-1350 (clone_mnt copies mnt_group_id from the old mount; set_mnt_shared only if it has one); mount_namespaces(7) "Shared subtrees"; unshare01.sh:145-146
- Suggested action: in setup, make the tmpdir its own shared mount (`mount --bind . .; mount --make-shared .`), or TCONF when findmnt shows the tmpdir mount is not shared. Read the expected ids from /proc/sys/kernel/overflow{u,g}id.
- Verification (phase 2, run on real hosts): **CONFIRMED** via RUN,CONTAINER. HPE: ltprun unshare01.sh 8/8 TPASS (/ is shared under systemd); ltprun unshare --mount --propagation private unshare01.sh -> 'unshare01 6 TFAIL: unshare --mount --propagation shared mount --bind dir_A dir_B did not get bind info' (passed 7 failed 1) on a correct kernel

### testcases/cve/cve-2025-21756.c  (runtest: cve/cve-2025-21756)
- Category: FRAGILE
- Confidence: high (phase 1: medium)
- Claim under test: vsock keeps socket binding until destruction (fix fcdd2242c023); kernel must not taint/crash.
- Problem: The test binds to VMADDR_CID_LOCAL, which requires the vsock loopback transport. When it is not registered (CONFIG_VSOCKETS_LOOPBACK=m and vsock_loopback not loaded, which is common on bare metal), bind() returns EADDRNOTAVAIL. vsock_bind() then reports TBROK, not TCONF. The TCONF branch keys off EINVAL ("VM socket is not supported"), but in __vsock_bind() EINVAL means "already bound" or an unsupported socket type, not that vsock is missing. The result is a false TBROK on correct kernels.
- Evidence: cve-2025-21756.c:138-142, :155; net/vmw_vsock/af_vsock.c:730-741 (vsock_find_cid needs transport_local for CID_LOCAL), :911-912 (-EADDRNOTAVAIL)
- Suggested action: add `.needs_drivers = (const char *const []){"vsock_loopback", NULL}` (or modprobe it), and map EADDRNOTAVAIL to TCONF.
- Verification (phase 2, run on real hosts): **CONFIRMED** via RUN,READ,VIRT. VIRT (KVM guest, vsock+virtio transport loaded, no vsock_loopback) as-is: 'cve-2025-21756.c:38: TBROK: bind() error: EADDRNOTAVAIL (99)'. HPE: TPASS when vsock not loaded (socket() autoloads net-pf-40 incl. vsock_loopback); after rmmod vsock_loopback with vsock core loaded: same TBROK EADDRNOTAVAIL

### testcases/kernel/controllers/cpuset/cpuset_memory_pressure_test/cpuset_memory_pressure_testset.sh  (runtest: controllers/cpuset_memory_pressure)
- Category: FRAGILE
- Confidence: medium
- Claim under test: cpuset.memory_pressure reports a non-zero rate for the cpuset whose
  tasks caused memory pressure, and zero for others / when disabled.
- Problem: The metric increases only in __perform_reclaim(), i.e. when an allocating task
  enters direct reclaim. Tests 4-6 require a non-zero value after
  allocating MemAvailable-20 MB. MemAvailable is defined as memory available "without
  swapping", and kswapd may free page cache fast enough that the hog never enters direct
  reclaim, which gives a false FAIL. The hog in sub_cpuset has mems=0 but is sized
  from system-wide MemAvailable. `check` requires 2 nodes, so that is about 2x node 0's
  memory. This forces cpuset-constrained OOM, which may kill unrelated node-0 tasks; the
  hog's exit status is ignored. Tests 3-4 also require the root cpuset rate to be exactly
  0 while any other system task in the root cpuset could hit direct reclaim during the
  hog run.
- Evidence: cpuset_memory_pressure_testset.sh:36-44 (usemem from MemAvailable), :156, :183,
  :229, :233 (-eq 0 -> TFAIL); /usr/src/linux/mm/page_alloc.c:4436-4447
  (`/* Perform direct synchronous page reclaim */ ... cpuset_memory_pressure_bump();`);
  kernel/cgroup/cpuset-v1.c:95,144 (fmeter_markevent on task_cs(current));
  Documentation/filesystems/proc.rst:1127-1129 (MemAvailable "without swapping").
- Suggested action: Size the hog from node-0 memory (node0/meminfo MemTotal) so it
  exceeds what node 0 can hold, which guarantees direct reclaim, or restrict it with a memcg
  limit. Accept root-cpuset noise, or move the reference tasks into a separate empty cpuset.
- Verification (phase 2, run on real hosts): **UNCHANGED** via RUN,READ. Cannot exercise: HPE/VIRT 'cpuset_memory_pressure 1 TCONF: Cpuset is not supported' (CONFIG_CPUSETS_V1 unset, both hosts have only node0 while check() needs 2 nodes). Re-read: cpuset_memory_pressure_bump() only on the direct-reclaim path (mm/page_alloc.c), hog sized from system MemAvailable; mechanism plausible but not reproducible here

### testcases/kernel/controllers/cpuset/cpuset_memory_spread_test/cpuset_memory_spread_testset.sh  (runtest: controllers/cpuset_memory_spread)
- Category: FRAGILE
- Confidence: medium
- Claim under test: With memory_spread_page=1, page cache of a cpuset task is spread over
  its mems; with 0 it is allocated on the local node.
- Problem: (1) Case `0 0 0,1 0` (spread=0, cpus=0, mems=0,1) expects all page cache on node 0,
  assuming CPU 0 belongs to node 0. This is never checked and is false on some
  topologies (CPU0 on another node, memoryless node 0). (2) Every non-target node must gain
  less than PAGE_SIZE*512/1024 kB (2 MB on 4K pages) of FilePages during the run. Any other
  file I/O on the system (journald, logs) breaks this. (3) freemem_check requires
  only 100000 kB MemFree per node, but the data file is 100 MiB (102400 kB). After
  drop_caches, normal zone fallback in the cpuset can then put pages on an unexpected node.
  (4) The TCONF message uses bash array syntax `${memsinfo[*]}` in a #!/bin/sh script, which
  fails with "Bad substitution" on dash, so the intended TCONF does not happen.
  TST_TOTAL=6 but test_spread_page2 reports a 7th result.
- Evidence: cpuset_memory_spread_testset.sh:298 (`0 0 0,1 0`), :49 (lowerlimit), :128
  (-lt 100000), :342 (${memsinfo[*]}), :26 (TST_TOTAL=6).
- Suggested action: Derive the expected node from /sys/devices/system/cpu/cpu0/node* (or
  pick a CPU on node 0). Raise the free-memory threshold above the file size with headroom.
  Make the "other nodes" tolerance relative to the 100 MB file. Fix the sh-incompatible
  expansion and TST_TOTAL.
- Verification (phase 2, run on real hosts): **UNCHANGED** via RUN,READ. Cannot exercise: 'cpuset_memory_spread 1 TCONF: Cpuset is not supported' on HPE/VIRT (CPUSETS_V1 unset, single node). Re-read confirms case '0 0 0,1 0' assumes CPU0 on node 0, 2 MB tolerance, 100000 kB vs 100 MiB file, ${memsinfo[*]} in #!/bin/sh (:342; harmless on Fedora where sh is bash), TST_TOTAL=6

### testcases/kernel/controllers/cpuset/cpuset_memory_test/cpuset_memory_testset.sh  (runtest: controllers/cpuset_memory)
- Category: FRAGILE  (secondary: WEAK)
- Confidence: medium
- Claim under test: anonymous/file/shm/hugetlb/mlocked memory of a task in a cpuset is allocated on cpuset.mems nodes; memory_migrate moves pages when the task moves or mems changes (17 subtests).
- Problem: Every step is synchronised only by `sleep 1` (lines 54-61, 251-261, 355-366, 476-487, 590-607, ...). The helper (cpuset_memory_test.c:343-350) blocks SIGUSR1/SIGINT with pthread_sigmask only after startup; a SIGUSR1 delivered before that kills the helper (default action) and the test reports a bogus node. Commit 77464232fde0 (Dec 2025) already had to add another sleep to paper over a race between allocation and `echo 0 > cpuset.mems`; on a loaded system the same ordering problem remains. Also test7 (lines 209-225) is byte-for-byte identical to test1 (lines 65-81) so it adds no coverage. Mounts v1 cpuset at /dev/cpuset, so on a v2-only host setup() TCONFs (fine).
- Evidence: cpuset_memory_testset.sh:54-61, 209-225; cpuset_memory_test.c:343-350 (mask set after process_options), git log 77464232fde0 "Fix race in multinode subtests".
- Suggested action: replace the sleeps with a readiness handshake (e.g. helper writes a line / uses tst_checkpoint after installing the mask, and prints after each step so the script can wait for output instead of sleeping); drop or repurpose test7.
- Verification (phase 2, run on real hosts): **CONFIRMED** via RUN,READ. Suite TCONFs here (CPUSETS_V1 unset). Mechanism shown in isolation on HPE: 'cpuset_memory_test --mmap-anon &' then SIGUSR1 without the script's sleep -> killed by default action (rc 138) in 2/10 runs (mask installed after process_options). diff test1 vs test7 bodies: only the function name differs
